A SUMMER DAY. •Tbe-sun beyond the distant hills Rose hr ugh the mist of night; 'Birds sang with joy their 'Latin lay, And hailed the flood of light. Qoolz phyrs from the rippling lake With perfumed breath passed by, And the orb of light in glory Marched through a cloudless sky. Full yellow a ,rnfields waving ripe, Danced in the noontide fair, And forest leaves In beauty curled Fanned by the gentle air. Slowly from the Meridian Passed on the god of day; ' *Glad earth, clad in herchoicest robes, Repaid his Relco m e d ray. It would be'e _ 'Bathetic death for Mr. Ruskin to see one o these vast and ungainly utilitarian temples of Ceres; but many a Lance-. shire operative and London tradesman gets his flour several shillings a barrel cheaper, and can thereby have more and better bread, because they exist and are ceaselessly busy. The works of elevating and shipping are not the most im- portant among those pertaining to the elevators, which are storehouses, first and foremost, where the grain product is held for a demand, or during the fluctuations of the market. Primarily-, therefore, they are granaries, the chief magazines of the nation, the reservoirs which compel Dantzio and Odessa to be reasonable.—Cities of the World for July.

Some years ago there was a vigorous attempt to establish the decimal system, bat the inert opposition of the public seems to have disheartened the reformers. Nothing is now heard of it, either as regards coinage or weights. But if we cannot establish a universal decimal system, we might do-something to provide that the same denomination of ex- i4ting measures shall be uniform through the country. Such is not now the case. Mr. Kains Jackson, in the Far- mer, refers. to, the subject this week. Dealing with the corn trade, he 'shows that Wheat is sold in Quarters of 504 lbs. Do not waste soap suds, but throw them around young trees, grape vines, and rose bushes. The British Dairy Farmers' Association will hold their next show in the first week of October in the Agricultural Hall. They have secured the hall for the next seven years fin- the purpose. VALUABLE SUGGESTION.—The latest proposition tcesatis- factorily kill two birds with one remedy is to train the Colorado potato bug to eat the phylloxera. The lattervill then pcison him, and the double riddance will be complete. A bottle Of carbolic acid should be kept in every farm- houreenot merely as a disinfectant, but as a wash for wounds and sores. For any purpose it should be dilated with water. Its power to destroy fungus growths makes carbolic acid invaluable in pruning orchards of pear, plum, or peach where blight or other disease is suspected. EARLY FOREIGN WHEAT.—Mr. Robert Imrie, farmer Bankhead of Balcurvie, Markinch, having secured seeds of a variety of wheat from Australia, had them sown along- side of, but separate from, his general crop of the same cereal about the middle of November, and at present the foreign variety shows the ears while the commoner sort is not yet swelling the shoot blade. EARLY POTATOES AT GIRTAN.—A considerable breadth a early potatoes in the neighbourhood of Girvan, which will be ready for raising in about ten days, have been sold to Glasgow dealers at £3O and £32 per imperial acre. The crops look well and promise an early and excellent field. The refreshing rains of the past few days have done much good to crops of every description. !INFLUENCE OF FERMENTING MANURES ON CULTIVATED Sous.— Experiments carried on at "Houghton Farm" during the summer of 1882 by Professor D. T. Penhallow, to .determine the influence of manures upon the temperature of soils, as compared with commercial fertilisers, showed that the temperature was raised from one-half to a whole degreeeby the use of stable manures. This, though seem- ingly a small matter, is yet of consequence, when it is re- membered that this variation may just measure the differ- ence_between frost and death to tender plants, and safety to the crap. The manure, too, had already been composted, and gave off less heat than much of the coarse, unfermented manure used by farmers. It was also found that soils fre- quently cultivated maintained a slightly more uniform tem- perature during the day, so that they were less injured by -severe drought. SHEEP-WORRYING BY DOGS.—A case of interest to farmers ,came before the County Court at Shrewsbury last week. rlt was an action brought by one farmer against another for the recovery of £5O, damages alleged to have been sustained by the defendant's dog worrying the plain- till's sheep. The evidence tendered on behalf of the latter was chiefly of a circumstantial character. No one saw the dog worrying the sheep. But some time after the poor animals had been discovered, torn and bleeding, the dog was seen with wool and blood-marks upon his body. Added to this fact was the evidence that this same dog race was not long before that engaged in worrying a flock of sheep on another farm, and the fact that since it had been got rid of the neighbourhood had been entirely free from sheep- worrying in any form. These circumstances the jury ap- pear to have considered sufficient to establish the plaintiff's claim and have, accordingly found for the full amount sought to be recovered. RABBITS ABROAD AND AT HOME.—The rabbit has before new in England played a political part somewhat out of proportion to its dimensions, and truly there have been places where the little rodont has played havoc enough. Wehave heard less about it of late, however, unless the northern claim of certain Scottish farmers to have a rabbit heleedefined to be something that is not a hole_, in order the better to trap him, be excepted, as proof that in North Britain' at least, agriculture and the rabbit are still at war. But that comparative peace still reigns in England would appear to follow from Sir William Harcourt's assurance to the See/ash remonstrants with the working of his Ground Game Act of 1880,'that-no complaints from any English farmer now reach the Home Office on this subject. It is very far otherwise, however, at this moment in some of our colonies. Rabbits are just now most serious intruders on the peace of Australians, and the latest Rabbit Act of New South 'Wales is a vigorous. specimen of the way in which the colonists are goaded to a war of extermination against this offender. +Tines of a round £lOO, or six months in duraneeseile, are, we read, proclaimed to be the fate of any rash poineesor ot, a live rabbit, or even a rabbit scalre Even in Canada it would seem the extermination of the, rabbit (or at least the rabbit of' English origin) has been voted, and means are being taken to rid the country of the.pest. Susan—Some new silos were filled at Mr. Bateman's farm at Brighttinsea on Monday, in the presence of a number of members of the EeseseAgricultural Society and other gentle- men interested. 'The silos, erected as an experiment by Mr. John Bateman, are three in number, and hold about 60 tons each, or 186stons in the aggregate. The total length of the range is 4lfta breadth I7ft., and height 13ft flin.,.decreas- ing lft. 7in..on the entire length. The partition walls which divide the one pit: into three are five inches in thickness, and constructed of concrete. A groove sunk drain in the floor runs 'down the centre. Thesilos are covered in with a corru- gated galvanized iron roof, which is constructed upon wheels, and is therefore easily movable. The structure was erected by Mr. =Edward Clarke, builder, of Great Bentley, the cost being about.,l.Bo. As the three silos hold 180 tons, the total primary cost of housing the grass and clover crops is estimated at Vs. 6d. per ton. We may mention that Mr. Clarke undertakes to convert empty cottages or disused barns into silos. On. the arrival of the visitors on Monday, they were courteously received at the farm by Mr. and Mrs. Bateman and conducted to the site of the new structure. Two of the silos were then empty, but one was being rapidly filled with fresh-mown and chopped clover. The clopping of the clover was being done, at the rate of seven or eight tons an hour, by one cf 'Bentall's C,E.L. steam-power chaff- cutters, driven with e-30in. pulley-1v a Rust and Proctor's eight horse power engine. The process of carting, filling the silos and treading down the greenstuffs by boy labour was watched for some time with considerable interest, Mr. Bate- man making all necessary explanations. THE SCOTCH CHEESE, FACTORIES IN CANADA.—Within an easy distance of Lancaster Ontario there are some eighty cheese factories, more than one-third of which are under the control of Mr. •M‘Pherson, the cheese king of Canada. Besides Mr.M‘Pilersonetbere are three other large operators, who own twentry-two, ten, and six factories re- spectively. The deliveries of milk are made only once a day, and it is required to beneseet and clean. it is warmed to 84 degs. Fahr. (or, if advanced towards souriog, to 88 degs. Fahr.) by means Of steam contained in a single straight pipe beneath the milk vat, which is made of nine, and placed in a wooden tub. The rennet (Hansen's extract) causes coagulation in forty-fiverisinutes. The curd is then . cut into half-inch cubes, and the whey allowed to drain off. -The cubes of curd are next stirred to keep them from ad- hering together, and their temperature is raised to blood heat. As soon as they are hard enough, one end of the vat is tipped down, and the whey, while yet sweet, drawn off through a strainer and tap. Meanwhile, and for some fifteen minutes afterwards, the cubes are stirred for the purpose of ,airing and assisting the whey to run off, which is con- sidered to be of great importance. The mass is then hauled the sides of the vats and left to settle. When dry enough to hold together, it is eat up and turned several times to set free the remainder of the whey, for which about a full hour is required. It is then paased through the mill and salted in the proportion of noes. of salt to 1001bs. of milk, after which it is placed in the cheese vat and stirred.. to admit as much air as possible, and finally it is .pressed. The factories are visited at irregular intervals by an expert, who tests the quality of the milk by means of graduated tubes and ice water—a process which occupies six hours. The seamless bandages used to encase the cheese are supplied to the factories cut off at proper -length and ready for uaa. All the crops seem to have made a determined effort to withstand the continued drought. The peas, which are the first to suffer, have maintained their verdure to the base, and the earliest sown will noye be ready for picking. We heard of some being picked ten days ago. They had no dcubt received some protection, but it is a proof of what these little artificial auxiliaries will do. Lettuce have cer- taiely been very impatient to increase their race by hastily "running to seed." This is diversity enough, one would imagine. Seven market.' .staples sold by five different weights. But the confusion does not end here. Mr. Jackson mentions that besides the i quarter of 5041b5. there are quarters of 4961b5. and 4801bs. in the wheat trade; that besides the quarter of 4481b5., quarters of 4161b5. and 4001bs. are known to the barley trade, and that oats are not only -sold by the quarter of 3361b5., but also by quarters of 3841b5., of 3041b5., of 3121b5., and of =32olbs. London sells cereals by the quarter and flour by the sack. Gloucester sells wheat by the quarter of 4961b5., oats by the quarter of 3121b5., and peas by the quarter of 4801bs. Belfast sells wheat and maize by the ton, but oats and oatmeal by the cwt., and flour by the 1961b5. weight. On this subject two deputations recently waited upon the -Government. The one urged that the cental should be made universal and compulsory, in order that the present system should not be interfered with; which Mr. Jackson aptly epitomises by saying :—One branch of the trade advo- cated a form of coercion most distasteful to Englishmen, rwhile another branch appeared to approve a state of things not very far removed from absolute chaos. The Govern- ment itself returns imported corn by cwts., but English corn by quarters of three different weights. Mr. Jackson thinks it not unreasonable to suggest that the Government should commence by using the cental or some other uniform idenomination in all their corn returns, and that the unani- mity of statisticians should precede the unanimity of traders.

THE BREEDING AND MANAGEMENT OF SHEEP.—Mr. J. H. Stephenson, Billingshield, -read a paper on this important subject at the last meeting of the Weardale Farmers' Club. inating pointed out that sheep were artificially produced, he observed that no other animal was worthy of so much attention to the farmer, because it was raised with so much ease, and in situations where other animals could not exist, making a better return than other animals, and to the na- tion, as supplying a staple article of food, and giving em- ployment to thousands of artisans by converting its wool into manufactured goods. The wool from English sheep was, perhaps, the strongest of any wool grown, but its value was less than that of other countries; English sheep being more esteemed for food. Owing to the introduction of colonial wool, he did not consider they could look for any improvement in the English wool trade,except in the coarser and longer kinds, such as the blackfaced sheep. Whilst ad- mitting there was room for improvement, he denied that that breed had deteriorated. There had been a falling off of about 25,000 sheep in Durham in the last four years, in Northumberland 100,000, and throughout the country 2,000,000; and as it was the only meat in which England could hold her own he recomasendeVarmers to pay more attention to it. He considered that just as English mutton excelled foreign, Yo blackfaced.emeelled other breeds. "The mutton," said one writer, "was mot so delicate as that of the sheep of Wales or the southdowns, but it . was more juicy, and had more of the venison savour, and was preferred to every other by those who were used Wit, and it was that point he held out as encouragement to the breeders of that class of sheep. (Hear, hear.) Ee preferred a sheep of me- dium scale, with the greatest possible substance, as being alike the most profitable to the breeder and the grazier. A few of the principal points were. a good head, with a bold appearance, and a good loin to stand well on the legs, which should not be too long. In choosing sheep for breeding pur- poses constitution was the chief thing to-be considered, and he advocated the selection of rams from fresh flocks or from animals not akin to their own, as ir.-and-in breeding had a tendency to make sheep soft. The best age for breeding stock sheep was from two to five years. In order to bring sheep to perfection they should be light stocked, the largest Inumber not being a criterion of profit. All land that was worth draining should be dr,ained, ae dry land suited sheep best. He believed more in improvingthe land so that sheep could "fend" for themselves than in -.supplying food by ar- tificial means, as all hand-feeding tended to make sheep less hardy and more dependent on man. (4plause.)—ln com- menting upon the paper, Mr. Chapman, Lea Side, pointed Out that in the London markets Welsh mutton was con- sidered the best, and brought the highest price. Whether the reason of that was because the blackfaced variety had not got known there or not he could not say.—Mr. Robin- son considefed the greatest drawback te,rearing sheep was the manner in which they were stinted, and so long as a heath land was undivided it would continue, to be detri- mental.
tREIGN INTELLIGENCE.'
Prince NapoleOn has returned to Paris. An international cattle show was opened at Hamburg on Tuesday. The Queen of Greece, accompanied by her snits, has ar- rived at Corfu.
From Bombay it is reported that the prospects of the crops are very favourable.
The Comte de Chambord died on Thursday at Frohs- dorf.

A telegram from Simla makes the remarkable announce- ment that the liovernment bas resolved to grant a large annual subsidy to the Ameer of Afghanistan. According to the weekly returns of the Bank of the Netherlands, the stook of gold has decreased by 650,000 florins.

It is stated from Rome that dissensions still exist between the Curia and the Society for the Propaganda respecting Irish affairs, due to the action of Mr. Errington. Cyclones raged over New York and New England on Monday night. One of them struck Cromwell, near Hart- ford, Connecticut, destroying almost every building in its path. Fourteen persons were killed.

- A. new Socialist journal, edited by the Russian agitator Lawroff, is about to appear at Geneva. It will be of a more conciliatory character than those hitherto published, acting as a sort of mediator between the Terrorists and the Socialists.

gine King of Saxony narrowly escaped death on Wednes- dAy. His Majesty was about to ascend in a factory " hoist " at Plauen, when an accident happened to the machinery by which the Governor of the district was killed and the mana- ger of the works seriously hurt. The King, who was in the 'moist at the time, escaped uninjured. The revenue of the colony of Victoria for the past year amounts to £5,600,000, being an increase of £12,500 Com- pared with the previous twelve months. Daring this period the customs increased by £74,250, and the receipts from railways by £123,000. On the other hand, the territorial revenue shows a decrease of £146000. The elections to the Bohemian Diet have been completed. In the towns the Germans (Liberals) returned 44 candidates, against 43 returned by the Czechs (conservatives). The elections for the class of landed proprietors were held on Wednesday. The general result is that the Diet will con- tam 167 Czechs and -75 Germans.

On Wednesday, being the Fourth of July, the anniversary of American Independence, the "stars and stripes" were hoisted over the American Consulate, and the warehouses of various American shipping firms in Manchester. Beyond this there was no outward observance of the day. The duties of the American Cousulate are at present being• dis- charged by Mr. J. T. Doyle, in the temporary absence of Colonel Shaw.

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENTS IN AMERICA.—The Phila- delphia correspondent of the Times, telegraphing on Mon— day night, says :—" A train on the Rochester and Pittsburgh Railway in North-Western Pennsylvania broke in two on a steep grade early on Sunday morning, and the front cars rushing down, crushed a passenger coach at the rear, killing six and injuring ten. A train on the Pittsburgh and 'Fort Wayne Railway at Chicago on Sunday night ran into a street tramcar at a grade crossing, and crushed it, killing three passengers and wounding several." A "demonstration" in favour of universal autXraxe took place in Brussels on Monday night. Several thousand per- sons formed a procession and went to the house of the President of the Chamber, where they left an address "demanding" the-immediate concession of the widest pos- sible suffrage. The'people afterwards visited the houses of the Ministers and demanded their resignation. The Times correspondent says the manifestation is generally considered as an attempt to certain disappointed politicians, whom the country obstinately refuses to take at their own estimate, to substitute mob rule for parliamentary institutions Two seronauts who ascended in a balloon at Courtrai, in Belgium, on Tuesday evening, have involuntarily accom- plished what M. L'Heste's most vigorous effort failed to achieve. Their intention was to go to Liege or Cologne, but when over Louvain they encountered an easterly cur- rent which carried them over Ostend, and, to their great alarm, out to sea. Suddenly they began to descend, and they feared that they would drop into the Channel; but.by throwing overboard large,quantities of ballast they again ascended, passed over Dover, and finally came to earth at Bromley, in Kent, where they were treated with marked hospitality, and experienced no slight relief at their timely escape.

THR DYNAMITE FACTION IN AMERICA.—About a thou- sand persons were present at a meeting in New York to raise money for Mr. Ford's "Martyrs' Fund." Mr. Sheridan delivered a speech in which he openly advocated the assas- sination of English officials in Ireland, and the meeting "endorsed" his recommendation to use dynamite or any other means of "bringing England to her knees." The speeches were exactly such as might be expected from the disciples of Rossa, but it is a little curious to find that Daniel Curley, who offered to become approver but found that he had been anticipated by Carey, is included in the list of "heroes who have died for their country." Sheridan, Walsh, and others will find, we believe, that their "brave words" will have little influence in Ireland. STEAMING THROUGH 160 Maltz OF Ice. Particulars have just been received of the steamer Ontario, which in the last outward volvage from the Mersey met with large ice floes in the straits of Belle Isle. Ste steamed through the ice until at last it became so dense that she could not move even with the help of hawsers. In this condition she re- mained for four Cays. During this time she spoke the schooner Enilly S. Muse off Port Esquimaux, and supplied her with a quantity of provisions, as she was short. The Ontario had on board a large number of passengers, who were happily landed,in excellent health. As appreciation of thetcomluct of the . uptain, officers, and .crew during the period they were ice-bound, the passengero presented them with a testimonial. The steamer is said to have passed through no fewer than 160 miles of ice. ALLEGED MURDER-TEAT. IN Partts"--Theiallowing extra- ordinary story is sent by the Paris correspondent of the Daily Caronicle :—The mystery surrounding a prisoner at Mazas, named Matteau, who obstinately refused to give any particulars, is now clearedzap. The accused waa recognised by other prisoners taken into Isustody, and the police have continued their investigations, flndinc, out a most extraor- dinary conspiracy to, corotnit wholesale murder. The mother of IlEarteau and some young women of diszeputable character are ;implicated. Marteau hired a housezaear the , Boulevard Menilmontant, an had a gang of well-dressed 1 young women to persuade men of wealthy appearance to visit them. In a dark passage there was a trap-door, com- municating with a cellar, in which, horrible to relate, there were large knives, newly sharpened, coarse sponges, ad a tub to receive the blood of the victims. Happily the arrest of a' Captain" Marteau has put an rod to this hideous plot. Several young women. have already given evidence to the juge.d'instruction.

-THE CHARGE AGAINST THE KHEDUE.—The documents dealing with the charge made against the Khedive by Lord Randolph Churchill, were sent to Mr. Gladstone, on Satur- day. They consist of five memoranda, the first being a general statement of the case, the second a review of the corroborative evidence in the Blue Book; Nos. 16 and 17, 1882, and No. 4, 1883. The third memorandum deals with the alleged suppression of the inquiry into the massacres of Alexandria; the fourth relates to the steps taken by the English Consul for arming the Europeans at Alexandria previous to the mas3acres ; and the fifth depicts the char- acter of the Khedive as illuatrated by his conduct before and after the bombardment. Then follows an affidavit of M. John Niuet and two further supplementary statements by him ; also an affidavit and supplimentary statement by M. Sabunji, an associate of Arabi's before the revolution. Then come four depositions by witnesses whose names are for the present suppressed. The papers are concluded by two letters from Mr. Blunt and Mr. Broadley to Lord R. Churchill narrating how most of the circumstances set forth in the, documents enclosed came to their knowledge. The whole consists of over 80 pages of printed matter.—Times.

THE CAMPBELLS. [Published by Mr. .E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavisteek-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission]. (BREADALBANE AND CAWDOR BRANCHES.) An estate a hundred miles long cannot be passed by un- noticed. A man able to walk along a tract of his own land as lengthy as the distance between London and Warwick must have enormous 'power—power of depopulation and expatriation over a large number of people. And in the case before us that power has been exercised.• Although the Duke of Argyll is the head of the Camp- bells, the Earl of Breadaibane has an equal income, and more than double the number of acres. In Argyll alone he owns more land that the Duke, no less than 179,225 acres, and in Perth 193,504 acres—total, 372,729, with a rental of £49,931. The trustees of the-late Marquis of Breadal- bane also hold 65,629 acres in these two counties—rental, 48,662. These Campbells are descended from Colin, younger son of Sir Duncan Campbell of Lochow, upon whom his father settled the estate of Glenorchy, in Argyll. How Glenorchy came to the Campbells I cannot say with certainty. Accord- ing to one account it was acquired by a marriage according to another it was anciently held by the Chief of the Mc.Gregors, and was acquired by the Campbells either through confiscation or conquest. Somewhat later the King granted to Colin the Barony of Lawers. His second wife was a kinswoman, daughter and co-heir of Lord Lorne, through whom lee acquired a third part of that lordship, which, as my readers will remember, had been legitimately obtained by a previous marriage. One of his descendants, who was created a baronet by James VI., also was made by that monarch hereditary keeper of the forests of Mamlorn, Bendaskerlie, &c. The third baronet, Laird of Glenfalloch, married the daughter of Sir Lachlan Mackintosh, captain of the Clan Chattan. The fifth baronet, being chief creditor of the Earl of Caithsess, obtained a disposition of his whole titles and estates, and at his death was created Earl of Caithness; but, it having been decided that the dignity in question belonged to the rightful heir, he obtained, in 1681, the title of Earl of Breadalbane. At the death of the third Earl, in 1782, the title and estates passed to a distant kinsman, who was subsequently created Marquis of Breadal- bane. At the death of his son the Marquisate expired, and the Earldom and estates passed to another distant kins- man. Let us look at the manner in which the Campbells of Breadalbane have treated their hundred-mile-long estate. In the Statistical Account of Scotland I find allusions to the depopulation of the lands to convert them into sheep farms, but, of course, in cautious and guarded terms. About five- and-twenty years ago, however, a Perthshire laird with whom I am personally acquainted, wrote a book on "The Barriers to the National Prosperity of Scotland," in which passing reference was made to the Breadalbane evictions. The second Marquis of Breadalbane wrote a lame answer in a local paper, which happily provoked from his antagonist a more detailed statement, in regard to which no answer at all appeared. The principal facts therein brought out I now repeat. As late as 1793 the Breadalbane estates furnished 1,600 soldiers; sixty years after they could not have pro- duced more than 1-50. At a time when the highest military authorities express their regret as to the number of boys we have to send into the field, we may well lament the loss of those stalwart Highlanders, whose forefathers-so freely shed their blood in fighting the battles of England. But Mr. Alister goes into detail. He states that in Glenqueich, where the same families had been tenants for 400 years, almost all were swept away, the 60 families having been reduced to four or eve ; that the:4o or 50 families inhabiting the braes of Taymouth and Tullochyoule were all expatri- ated; that in Glenetive, where were formerly 16 tenants, not one was left; that in the island of Ling 25 families had given place to one; that the population of Glenorchy had been reduced by one-half; that in three other places, which formerly were tenanted by -50 families in all, only one family was left; and that several other " toons " had been cleared of from 10 to 14 families each. In twenty years from 1834 no less than 500 families had been cleared off the soif. He further states that the land in front of Kenmore, the land around Drummond Hill, and Black Mount had all been converted intoaleer forests. The latter alone contained nearly 100,000 acres of fine pasture-land capable of grazing 70,000 sheep, instead of the -3,000 which were there on a portion of it. Well might Sir Walter Scott write: "In too many cases the Highlands have teen drained, not of their superfluity of population, but of the whole mass of the inhabitants, dispossessed -by an unrelenting avarice, which will be one day found to have been as short-sighted as it is unjust and selfish." Of the selfishness of the policy which drove men out to make room for sheep and deer there can be no question; of its injustice I have already spoken when dealing with the Leveson-Gowers. The ancestors of these poor people had been Eying • industrious lives in these glens for ages; it was only by what Mr. Hill Barton calls "iniquitous legal jugglery," that the lords Obtained the right to dispossess them. Their expatriation was spoliation of the worst kind. Their descendants in the American Glenorchy. which was named after the old home, might well saY with Nicol We sow the corn and hold the plough, We all work for our living; We gather nought but what we've sewn, All else we reckon thieving. The lords of Breadalbane held a different opinion. By the way, I presume that the rentals furnished for the Land- owners Return do not include the rents of seer forests, but it would be desirable that the matter should be made clear by these who are able to give-definite information. The Earl of Cawdor is descended from a cadet of the great house of Campbell. The property he possemes has been ae-juired by successive fortunate-marriages. Be owns • in—
Nairn Carmarthen Pembroke . invents Cardigan ..,
Total.. With a rent•roll of L 44,644,

A younger son of the Earl of Argyll married the daughter and heiress of Sir John Calder of Calder, or Cawdor, in Nairnshire. At Cawdor Castle they used to show the very room in which King Duncan was murdered. Conside4ing that Duncan was not murdered at all, and that the Castle was not built till some hundreds of years after his death, this must have been a valuable relic of antiquity. They even showed theibOd on which the King slept, but unfor- Annately that was burned. Later, one of these Campbells married the sister and heiress of Mr Gilbert Lort, of Stack- pole Court, Pembrokeshire. It is uncertain how the Lorts acq-uired the estate. The eldest son of this marriage con- tracted an alliance with another Welsh heiress, Mary Pryse. His grandson was created Baron Cawdor, and the second Baron obtained an Earldom.

The Earl of Cawdcr is one of those Welsh Tory land- owners who, in virtue .of the acres they possess, have until lately managed to secure, in several of the Welsh Counties, members who vote in direct opposition to the principles of the majority of the voters, _

It is..wor-thy of notice that there are no less than twenty- eight other Campbells, each owning 5,000 acres and up- ward, for the most part in Scotland, the total amount being 538,861 acres. The Campbello, therefore, hold between them no less than 1,253,989 acres. At the time of the passing of the first Reform Bill, sixteen Campbell placemen and pen- sioners divided £24,000 between them annually.

A jury in Alabama had been empanneled in the case of a man charged with killing his wife. The evidence was positive and conclusive, leaving not a doubt of his speedy conviction. To the amazement of all, the jury, after a short absence, returned a verdict, "Guilty of horse-steal- ing!" The judge, astonished, asked an explanation, stating that the indictment was not for horse-stealing, but man- slaughter. The foreman, with his hand upon a huge law- book, and with an amusingly dignified air, informed the court that "it was not a case of manslaughter, but woman- slaughter, for which the law made no provision; but being satisfied the man deserved to be hung, they had brought in a verdict of horse-stealing, which, in that county, would be sure to swing him !" TRlPLETS.—Mackintosh had tosendure a fierce fire of puns and jokes on one occasion. He was on circuit and anxiously expecting certain information of the utmost domestic im- portance, when at Huntingdon the news arrived. A fine healthy boy had just been born to him. When he reached Cambridge there was another letter from home. It an- nounced the birth of a second boy. At Bury another letter was awaiting him announcing the birth of a third boy. The letters had been written successively, immediately after the births; but the second just missed the post, which the first just caught, and the third had been delayed on the road. George Wilson gravely proposed the health of Mrs. Mack- intosh and her three sons, Grotius, Puffendorf, and Vattel. —London Society. TUE PRICES OF SOME HISTORICAL FISR.—We in Eng- land, with the sea all around us, naturally expect to get our fish cheaper than any other nation; as a matter of fact it is cheaper in London and other of our cities and towns than it is in almost any capital of Europe, barring only those of the Northern nations. Order a salmon-cutlet or a sole in Paris, and the chances are very great, in respectable, though not the highest-class restaurants, that you will have to pay from three to five or more francs for your audacity. If it is fresh, congratulate yourself. Oysters have sold for as much as a paper rouble—about a shilling—a-piece, in St. Petersburg. But what are these to the prices obtained in ancient Roma! The equivalent of six pounds sterling was a common outlay for one pound of fish; some mullets, of which history makes mention, were sold for the astonishing high figures of £4B, £64, and £240! Fish .was half the time a luxury for millionaires only. There were human hogs, too, in those days, as in these days; the Emperor Vitellius is said to have got through twelve hundred oysters at a sitting. Though doubtless an exaggeration, it evi- dently meant an extravagant fondness on his part for the delicious bivalve. It was by no means an uncommon weak- ness, then as now. Seneca, the wise, could manage his hun- dred or so; and Latin poets sung its praises. Cicero boasted that he had learnt contentment in a state of modest retire- meat, which debarred him from the enjoyment of eels and oysters, but if he did not find a course or two of some rare fish at the entertainments to which he was invited, he was, all the same, rather apt to make a note of the deficiency. There is a story of one Cassidorus who sold his slave in the morning that he might sup on a murgena, the purchase of which cost him all he got by Ole bargalg.—" The Fisheries of the World" for July.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

RA SrDERTLY stools throw up a number of shoots from which the best should be selected, five or sevei being suffi- cient for each stake, and when they are trained to wires in a continuous row the sh.oots should be Bin. apart. It is usual to allow all growths OKA are produced to remain until the autumn, when the surplus are removed at the same time as the old canes. It is obV:ous that all the shoots derive their nourishment from one secrce. Assuming their tatal to be twelve, it is only reasonable to conclude that if six are re- moved at an early period the remainder will be supplied with so much more nutriment. Apart from this, .early thinning admits sun and air to consolidate and ripen the wood: If the raspberries have not had a top dressing •iz the winter or spring they should receive one now; they make a quantity of surface roots annually which require protection ,from solar influences.

FRONT GARDRN.—The okief work here will be staking and tying those plants supposed to grow upright, and .r)eg- ging those that trail upon the ground, such as verbenas and petunias. Those who may not have followed our advice earlier in the year will do well to hazard a small sowing of Delphiniums, Wallflowers, ..fiweet William, Aquilegia Columbines, and Canterbury Bells. All seeds will come up quickly arter the rain has soaked the ground. The follow- ing plants, suitable for a front garden, are now in flower, and thong: they have been introduced to this country be- fore the birth of the present centary we only see fragments of them here and there :—lris of Flag, Pinks, whitd. and mottled; Campanulas, Anemone, Tradescantia, Larkspurs, Centranthus, Rubra and Alba, and,the White Rocket. The latter is most 'easily propagated by cutting a plant partly down when the flowers are past their best. Numerous side shoots will then be emitted, which when 3in. to 41n. long will be suitable for -cuttings, and may be inserted in the border near the plant, cr elsewhere.

THE WiNn&w.—Plants in the window are grown under the most unfavourable artificial conditions. The worst is perhaps the absence of a supply of fresh air, which is mani- fest in the elongated joints and the petioles of the leaves or •leaf-Aalks. Accumulated dust on the foliage is another. The last we shall name is common to all plants grown in pots, whether in the window or the most costly constructed ! greenhouse i.e., the limited area allowed to the roots to grow in. It is evident that no additional Mid pabulum can be supplied to the ,roots after they are placed in the pot; so whatever nourishment we wish to supply them with must reach the roots in a liquid form. When we sprinkle the surface of the soil with Clay's fertilisor or Standen's manure, which, by the way, are the two .best artificial manures extant for this purpose, the result is .the same; the virtue is washed from the fertilising ingredients by one watering after another, whereby all the roots are benefited. Good honest manure water,can be made from the excrement of the horse. Its use is objectionable in dwelling-houses on account of the offensive smell for some hours after it is applied. Plants cannot ,be brought even to a standard of mediocrity without stimulants. Space will not allow at Present to enter fully into details as to the proper time to apply them to various plants. Should we not shortly recur to it, any reader can have any.apecial information supplied , to 'him in this column. I

div.head: ' THE CHOLERA IN EGYPT.
div.p: ' THE CHOLERA IN EGYPT.

An Alexandria telegram, dated Thursday, says :—The number of deaths from cholera at Damietta yesterday was 111. At Mansurah there were 46 cases and 43 deaths, at Chirbin 4, at Port Said 3, and at Samound 4. There were o cases here.

div.head: TONQUIN QUESTION.
div.p: THE TONQUIN QUESTION.

It is stated that the Chinese Government have concluded important contracts in the United States for the purchase and immediate delivery of a considerable quantity of arms, and for several ironclad transports and torpedo boats. The latest intelligence received at the Foreign. Office tends to demonstrate the determination of China to prepare for the eventuality of war while prolonging negotiations to gain time.

Li Hung Chang, the Chinese Commissioner at Shanghai, has definitely rejected the terms proposed by the French Government in relation to Tonquin, and has referred M. Tricou to the Foreign Board at Pekin. M. Tricou on his part declares that whatever the decision of the Chinese Government may be France will reserve to herself perfect liberty of action.

Evan Evans, a bright little Welshman, in one of the Welsh settlements of Pennsylvania, is very fond of playing the harp, but complains that he cannot improve for the want of proper instruction. A waggish Yankee conse- quently advised him to subscribe for Harper's Magazine, which he did at once, supposing it to be a publication in- tended specially for harpers. Meeting Evans some time ago we asked him how be liked his magazine, and he re- plied : "Tat Yankee is a great rogue; but ta Harper is a vera goot book."

AN EXTRAORDINARY MEMORY.—A teacher of mathema- tics, named William Lawson, who died at Edinburgh in November, 1757, on one occasion, to win a wager made by his patron, undertook to multiply regularly in succession the numbers from one to forty, without other aid than his memory. He began the task at seven o'clock in the morn- ing, and finished at six in the evening, when he reported the product, which was tested on paper, and found to be correct. It made a line of forty-eight figures, and a fair copy of it long occupied a place on the wall of his patron's dining- room, for which it was framed and glazed. It may be added, that in the course of the day on which the mental calculation was made Mr. Lawson received his pupils as usual, and gave them their ordinary 'lessons in Latin.— London Society. - It is necessary, during hot weather ta avoid beverages likely to heat or stimulate the system Cocoa, deprived of the super- &tills oil, and guaranteed ab,•olutely pure, is am soothing, sustaining. and refreshing beverage Be sure that you ge :bory s eccaa F3sEnce when you itsi:k for it, a, imiLati ,ns a!, • Pen nu!hed by 4:oplcecpers for the rake, oi extra profit .Alakers bi2pec!2lffppi.Dtsnect 1.-f) t!!? 9t4TD.—..44vf.

LYMM LOCAL BOARD, The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board- room, Lymm, on Thursday evening. There were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewhurst, Rogers, Callender, Gibbon, Appleton, Thomason, Ridgway (clerk), and Mullard (assistant clerk).

PROGRESS OF THE SEWERAGE SCHEME. Messrs. WILSON and MuLLJNER reported that the whole of the works on the outfall land were now complete except- ing the receiving basin, the irrigation channels, and prepar- ing for planting sziers. The 15-ilch main was nearly complete, except the portion at Statham Pools and the lift- ing of the Rush Green sewer. The bridge at Statham Pods would not be ready for another fortnight, and as the farmers would probably then be carting hay they had considered it advisable to delay the erection until the hay season was over. On the 24th May extra no. 9 for the necessary earth works and sodding to banks on Mr. Ross's land north of the railway was authorised by the Board. Mr. Brazendale was proceeding with this work. There were also two small extras, namely, one for wattling a short length of Done Bank and the other a short length of concrete foundation in Peter Warbur- ton's field. These were extras Nos. 10 and 11. The Lymm branch was laid from the junction with the 15-inch main to a point near the canal at Lymm. The work in connection with the tender of Mr. Brazendale, accepted on the 26th June, for the proposed alteration between the mill and the canal was now in hand at the ironfounders. This would be extra No. 12. Extra 13 would be far altering the position of automatic flushing Chambers from Mr. Warburton's field to Rush Green opposite Mr. Parkinson's house and build- ing automatic flushing chamber at the head of house, sewer as passed by resolution of March 18th. In coanection with Statham Lane, the arrangements with the Railway Co. were practically agreed to ; they were only awaiting the signed agreement.—Mr. ROGERS asked if those mentioned would be the only extras, and Mr. WILSON replied that they would, with the exception of one or two of a minor charac- ter.—Aresolution was passed that the road along Poole- lane to the canal bridge be closed during the time required for laying the sewer. a A SANITARY IMPROVEMENT. The NUISANCE INSPECTOR reperted that during the month six of Fowler's patent closets had been put down on cottage property at Booth's Hill. Since they had been put down the tenants of the cottages said thay could not perceive the least offensive smell whatever, and they expressed them- selves highly sitisfied with the change. The new closets seemed to be specially adapted for properties where privies were placed in small yards and were very much confined, such as those at the Rookery and others situate in Cherry- lane. If some means could be devised by which the im- proved system could be adopted in lieu of the present cess- pit privies in the places referred to it would most certainly be a very great sanitary improvement. He had inspected the slaughter houses and found them clean and satisfactory. ItooEas spoke in glowing terms o" the great advantages to be gained from the adoption of the improved system of closets.—The CHAIRMAN said it was a pity a few did not take up the question and put. a number of new closets on their property.—The CLERK remarked that suggestions had been sent out to owners of property and to anyone to whom they thought they would be of use.—Mr. PEWHURST asked how long it would be before they could connect with the sewer, and the CLERK replied that though they might connect They would not be able to use tbe outfall this year.—Mr. "DEWHURST said there was no doubt that after people had used the new system they would see that it worked well and then they would recommend it to their neighbours.-- Mr. ROGERS :Itis a final and effectual improvement. 1 tbink that the landlords will soon see that is to their bene- fit to adopt it.—Mr. APPLETON asked if after the system was adopted the Board would have to remove the ashes.—Mr. ROGERS : Oh no, not atall.—Mr. APPLETON said the Board would have to find a place for them, and he thought they would have to remove them.—The CHAIRMAN said that sup- posing the Board had to clear away the cinders it would be easier to do that than to clear away the mixed matter. He did not think that affected the question.—Mr. APPLETON: It's a strange thing to me that if these closets are so bene- ficial there were not more of them where we went to.—The CHAIRMAN: They said there were 300, and they have put more in since.—Mr. APPLETON: But how many cottages were there ? Only 3,000 !—The CHAIRMAN: I aaresay the place We Saw was the worst.—Mr. APPLETON: He said there were worse places than that.—The CHAIRMAN : Ihey could not he much worse. (Laughter.)—Mr. APPLETON said that in his opinion the new system would be a failure unless there was a plentiful supply of water.

THE SURVEYOR'S- REPORT. The SURVEYOR reported that during the past month the work of repairing the bridge across the canal had been attended to. A surface boarding of 2-inch red deal had been put down, and the pavement at the lower end of the bridge had been extended to a distance of 10 feet, but in order to make a good substantial approach it was necessary that the pavement should be continued a distance of 20 or 30 feet further down. About 170 lineal yards of 4-inch drain pipes had been put down in Mug-lane, with a view•to draining the road.

CLAIMS FOR COMPENSATION. . The CHAIRMAN said that Mr. Blinston had sent in a claim for .£2O, and Mr. Marsh one for £l5, as compensa- tion for giving up land for sewerage purposes Nrithout notice.,—Mr. DEW/IT:R.BT : I think the matter has come to the point at which it ought to be settled. I don't think there is any probability of getting the claims reduced any further.—lt.was then decided, on the motion of Mr. DEW- Huaer, seconded by Mr. CALLENDER, that the sums claimed be pzia.—The following persons also made claims for dam- ages to.crops, 4r.0., caused during the construction of the sewerage works, and it was decided, on the motion of Mr. THOML6ON, seconded by Mr. GIRBON, that the claims be paid :—John Forster, Rash Green, £7 ; Thomas Hutchin- son, Statham, £1 103. ; Joseph Tickle, Pool-lane, Stathani, ; Samuel Appleton, Statham, £2 103. ; George Clarke, Statham, 15s. ; James Sharpies, Statham, £l, Peter War- hort,n and Leigh Warburton gave notice that they would claims for damages.

BOARD AND EYE LANES. A letter was read from Mr. Collin Mclver stating that the Board had put a good deal of wear and tear on the roads in Eye Lanes, which are repaire:', by voluntary rates, and that the Board would be ezKpected to contribute its share towards the repair of the road.—Mr. ROGERS said he thought it was nothing but right that the Board should bear its share of the rate.—Mr. TROMAGON said the Board had done a great deal for the Statham farmers, and he thought there was no necessity for their asking for what they had.—Mr. ROGERS said there were many in ttathatn who had to contribute to- wards the repairing of the road rho did not receive any benefit from what Mr. Thomason referred to.—Mr. DEW- HURST said the Board were cot, asked to pay the whole of the rate.—The CHAIRMAN: it will be 52. or 63. per year.— Mr. DEWHIIRST : It is a trifling amount, and it will be easier to pay it.—The subject then dropped.

RESIGNATION OF MR. TAYLOR. The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Taylor, as a member of this Board, has just sent in a letter tendering his resignation, but it is written in such terms that I don't think I shall be justified in reading it to the Board. I hope 7,70 u will accept it as read.—Mr. ROGERS : I propose that his resignation be accepted, Mr. Chairman—The CHAIRMAN was understood to say that it would be better for someone else to make the proposition.—Mr. DEwHuRST then proposed, asd Mr. GIBBON seconded, that Mr. Taylor's resignation be accepta, and the proposition was passed.—The letter was afterwards passed round thetable.—The CHAIRMAN: It is a letter I cannot take the responsibility to give to the public. At the next meeting I shall propose that Mr. Woolley be elected to fill the vacancy, if he is willir.g. There was no other business of public interest.

The postoffice announces that a postage and inland revenue stamp, value 2s 6d, available for postage, telegraph, and in- land revenue purposes, is now being issued, and will shortly be obtainable from all postmasters, i.tc. VEGETABLE VILLAINS.—With regard to their pilfering habits, such plants are usually portioned off into great groups. They either attach themselves to other beings and absorb their juices, in which case they form a mighty host of plants of prey usually known as parasites; or they seek their nutrimentand find it, in dead and decaying organisms, and are then known as saprophytes, a somewhat hard word to begin with, for which I cannot find a popular equivalent, but which merely signifies plants that grow on decomposing matter. All land plants that are not blessed with a true green colour belong to one or other of these groups, and are villains in their various degrees. They make no effort to free the air from the gaseous impurity that haunts it, but, like animals, they keep fouling it instead. With a very few exceptions, all of them subsist on organic matter in some form, and this they usually draw from the plants, living or dead, on which they grow, or from decaying matter in the soil. But many of these vegetable villains run into half- I honest vagaries, and succeed in raising themselves slightly above the common ruck. If they cannot seize and break up carbonic-acid gas, they may do a little towards atmospheric purification of a kind by laying fast hold on such organic particles as are floating in the air or brought to them in falling moisture. Plants such as these are sometimes found growing on barren sand, on hard gravel, on parapets of bridges, on leaden bisterns, on plastered walls, on slag, and in like inhospitable places, where they are compelled to turn mainly to the atmosphere and trickling moisture for food. Some such haunt mines like phosphorescent ghosts, others make themselves at home on places like the dome of St. Paul's Cathedral. In a mass two feet in length, similar strange plants were one morning long ago found by a smith on a piece of iron that he had taken, on the previous night, red-hot from his fire and laid over his water-trough. Many similar vagaries they run into that would in the telling sound almost incredible. Indeed, the whole group of the siprohpytes is not to be accounted so utterly abandoned as that of the parasites. To these they are certainly nearly related, but there is more of the useful scavenger about them than of the useless thief. No sooner has death over- taken any plant than a host of them set to work to clear Away the now useless organism from the world, breaking down herbaceousness into putrescence, timber into touch- wood, and all at last into vegetable mould. Their mission is to seize upon decaying matter, and endow it with life in a new form; and thus out of rottenness often comes whole- someness, decay moulding itself into pleasant mushrooms, or into things unfit for human food perhaps, bit that may bring the blessings of abundance to many little living creatures. If such as are edible are to be considered villains, then people of delicate palate who smack their lips over some of them have a right to insist that these should be classed as dainty little rogues.—Good Words. The Exchequer returns from April let to June 13th show —Receipts, £20.798,738 ; expenditure, £20,571,100; balances, £8,243,832. Corresponding period of last year— Receipts, £19,976,756; expenditure, £20,502,692; balances, £4,877,503. At the Convocation of Canterbury, on Tuesday, the Bishop of Oxford expressed regret at having used words in- dicating the presence of immorality at the Salvation Army meetings, but he thought that the Salvationist officers should exercise greater vigilance over the morals of tlie young. At the Durham Quarter Sessions on Monday, a young man, named Thomas Higgins, who had been out on bail, was sentenced to six months' hard labour for bribing two telegraph messengers at Stockton on the Derby day. The prisoner gave the lads half-a-crown to tell him the winner, and half-a-crown to delay the delivery of the message until he got his money on. THE SAGACITY OF THE DOG. A striking instance of the fidelity and sagacity of the dog occurred at Milford Haven last week, when a boat containing two sergeants of the 23rd (Welsh) Fusiliers was swamped. Their names were Davies and Tay- lor, and the first-mentioned was the owner of a dog. While the men were struggling in the water, the animal caught hold of Taylor, but finding that it was not his master at mace let him go and swam to the other. The result was that Taylor was drowned, while the faithful dog supported Davies until rescue came from a passing steamer. BABY FARMING REVELATIONS.—An inquest was held OR Wednesday at the Court House, Raynharn, London, on the body of Charlotte Morgan, aged four years, who was starved to death by a baby farmer named Margaret Taite, who is now in custody charged with causing the death of the child. The deceased was placed in the care of the accused three months ago, and since then had become very emaciated. A few days back, from what the mother was told she com- municated with the police, and the deceased, with three other children which the accused had under her care, were removed to the Infirmary. They were partially insensible and covered with vermin. Everything was done for them, but deceased died on Saturday last. Dr. Roberts said de- ceased had died from starvation and gross neglects—The jury returned a verdict of Wilful murder" against the accused woman Taite, and she was fully committed. THE -SUNDERLAND DISASTER.—The coroner's inquiry into the circumstances of the Sunderland disaster has re- sulted in a verdict which will be generally endorsed. As to the actual cause of death there was no doubt, and the jury accordingly found that the children died of suffocation through the partial closing of the door on the landing; but how the door came to be fixed in its position they did not find evidence enough to show. They censured the giver of the entertainment for not having provided a sufficient number of persons to look after the safety of the addience, and found that a partnership existed between Mr. Fay and Mr. Coates, who shared the profits with Mr. Fay. They , recommended the removal of the door, and acquitted the caretaker of the ball of all blame, but thought that in future he should have instructions to show persons who engaged the hall all the modes of ingress and egress. EITRAORDINAY CONDUCT OF A CLERGYMAN.—The Rev. Robert Topham, vicar of Etruria, near Hanley, was on 'Tues- day summoned for having wilfully destroyed trees and plants in the Hanley Borough Cemetery. The reverend gentleman refusing, however, to obey the summons, In- spector Vicars and Sergeant Williams were sent for him to the vicarage. They were first informed that he was in the garden. Afterwards the servant told the officer that Mr. Tophem had told her to say he was not at home; and subse- quently, on further demanding his appearance, they were informed that he was ill in bed. On the magistrates being informed of this they at once issued a warrant for his arrest, and he was shortly afterwards taken into custody. When ' before the justices he prevaricated so seriously that the pre- siding magistrate observed he had told several untruths. He ought to have set a better example to the public, and the Bench would therefore mark their sense of his extraordinary conduct by inflicting the highest penalty the law would allow. THE REPRESENTATION or LIVERPOOL. Mr. James Samuelson has addressed to the electors of Liverpool a formal acceptance of the invitation recently sent to him on behalf of the labouring classes to contest the city at the next election. He will forego the position should a direct representative of labour be chosen as a candidate, but other- wise, while avowing himself a Radical, he will be willing to sink party considerations in dealing with questions strictly connected with labour, and • will reserve to himself liberty of action in great questions of reform. In thus taking time by the forelock Mr. Samuelson leaves no doubt as to his present intention to contest the seat at all hazards. —The question of running an Irish Nationalist for Liver- pool at the next general election is at present engaging the attention of a collimate° of influential Irish citizens. No- thing definite will be decided upon, however, until Mr. Pa- rnell is consulted, which will be done as soon as possible. It Is intended to conduct the election on the purity ticket as advocated and practised by the late Mr. William Simpson, and also by Mr. Healy in the late Monaghan contest. DISASTER TO A WHALER: SEVERAL LIVES LO3T.-011 Tuesday morning information came to hand at Liverpool of a shocking disaster to the whaling vessel Ellen Rizpab, by which about eight of her crew lost their lives, inch:Wing the chief officer. The intelligence was received from Wood's , Hole, United States, where the Ellen Rizpah arrived on the 20th till, and reported the sad affair. It appears that while the vessel was on her whaling cruise the captain and chief officer were each in command of a boat. Both of the men struck a whale simultaneously. Instantly the leviathan felt the harpoon she disappeared beneath the surface of the water with lightning speed. Unfortunately, the line attached to the.rnate's harpoon fouled, and thr boat. with all its accu- pants, were drawn beneath the waves. The boat was never afterwards seen, and, out of a crew of about nine hands, only one, a coloured man, succeeded in escaping, the remainder perishing. The name of the mate was Dunham, but the names of the other unfortunate men, as well as their number, were not given; but it was believed that there were about nine men in the small craft when she was taken under. THE LABOUR MARICET.—The state of the labour market remains about the same as last week. Building operations, tramway construction, and railway work continues very active, and labour is plentiful. In colliery districts, although work is plentiful, strikes are prevalent, and on Monday a large number of miners at West Bromwich and district eame out on strike against a proposed reduction in wages of 3d per ton. The North Staffordshire strike still continues, and the miners in other districts, especially Wales, are rendering support to the strikers. Shipbuilders and engineers in all parts are very busy. In the iron trade an average amount of labour exists, although in some parts agitation is going on, and masters find it difficult to keep up the standard of wages, owing to the continued low prices. At Newcastle-on-Tyne, in accordance with the slid- ing-scale arrangements, miners' wages have been advanced 21 per cent., and a further advance is probable. At Birm- ingham, in the heavy trade, machinery is going briskly, and most trades are active. At Sheffield, edge-tool and steel- making machinery manufacturers are very busy, and a steady demand for electro-plated goods and cutlery keeps workpeople fairly employed. At Wolverhampton there is 1 sufficient work on order to last some months. At Manches- ter locomotive builders are very busy, one firm alone having I just received an order to construct thirty tramway engines j for the Birmingham district. The textile trade shows no material change from last week. At Bradford spinners are well employed, and at Halifax machinery is fairly em- ployed and dyers of some classes of goods are busy, which perhaps explain.' the cause of the dyers at Pickle Bridge striking over a wages dispute of 25 per cent. The carpet trade also shows more activity. At Manchester the ware- houses manage to keep to full time. At Huddersfieleforders for next spring goods are being placed freely. At Kidder- minster worsted spinners and carpet manufacturers are busy. At Leeds, manufacturers are generally fully employed. At Leicester, spinners are fairly busy, and hosiery weaving shows somewhat more activity. The Nottingham lace manufacturers, although steadily employed, feel the effect of reduced prices. In the tin mining districts of the west increased labour is apparent, and districts are fortunately free from labour disputes. The boot and shoe trades in the various centres are quiet, work being. comparatively scarce. In agripultural districteall branches of labour are busy. Emigration continues fairly brisk.—The Labour News.

THE I ANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—In the iron market generally cheerful tone is maintained, and although the actual business doing is not large, makers are firm in their prices. In the pig-iron trade the recent buying having pretty well filled up the requirements of consumers there is a quietening down in the demand, but makers are so fully pold that they are indifferent about further orders at present. For Lancashire pig-iron makers still quote 45s to 45s 6d, less 21, as their minimum for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, but sales only to a limited extent are being made on this basis. In district brands 44s 103. to 45s 103, less 21, for forge and foundry delivered here are the lowest figures new quoted; a fair business could be done at about ed under these figures, but at the full rates buyers bang back. In the finished iron Itrade there is an improvement so far as shipping enquiries are concerned, with rather better prices offered- by buyers, but for home requirements the demand is still only dui?. Makers are steady in their pric2s, and there appears to be less underselling, but the reports that one of the leading Staffordshire firms had reduced their quotations 5s per ton were somewhat disconcerting in view or the firmer tone which has apparently been growing of late in this market. For delivery into the Manchester district quotations remain at £6 2s 6d to £6 5s for bars, £6 12s 6cl to £6 15s for hoops, and £7 17s 63.- and £8 to £8 5s per ton for sheets.—ln the coal trade business is dragging on slowly, .with the usual quiet demand for the time of the year. louse-fire coals meet with only a very slow sale, and in the Manchegter dis- trict the leading firms have made a reduction of 10d per ton on the delivered rates to consumers, but this does not affect the wharf or pit prices. In the Bolton district there have been reductions of 10d per ton in the wharf and delivered rates for all descriptions of coal except slack. The common classes of round coal meet with only a dull demand for home requirements, but for shipment there is a fairly good business doing. The usual railway contracts for steam coal_ have recently to a large extent been placed out, but the cornpanieg have not been able to cover their forward require- ments except at an advance of about 6d per ton upon last year's prices. Engine fuel, except some of the best sorts of slack, continues generally abundant, and although at a few of the Manchester collieries there is an advance of 5d per ton on slack it can scarcely be said that prices as a. rule are being more than maintained. At the pit mouth the ave- rage prices are as under :—Best coal, 9s; seconds, 7s ; com- mon round coal, 5s 6d to 6s; burgy, 4s 63 to ss; common slack, 2s 93. to 3s 3d ; good qualities, 35 63. to 4s; with beat sorts fetching 4s 3d to 4s Od per ton in some oases.

The accused gave the name of Samuel James, of no home, aged 84, and he was charged with begging at cab doors. On being searched there was found upon him a draft for £204 5s 9d, ten American 20 dollar notes, four 10 dollar notes, £5 in gold, one twenty dollar piece, three ten, eight five, and one one dollar piece, and 22s ad in silver, making in all over £276. TERRIBLE SCENE AT A RAILWAY STATION.—A farmer's wife and her three children attempted to cross the Great- Western Railway at Horrabridge station, on Tuesday, just as a train was drawing near. A porter, seeing their danger, rushed across the line, but the affrighted woman, instead of allowing herself to be pushed back, struggled with him. and all five were thrown down by the engine. One girl was caught by the guard and thrown aside without sustaining much injury. The others were all dragged for about fora, feet beneath the engine, having been caught by the fire-box. All were rescued alive, and will, it is believed, recover. PARLIAMENTARY TACTICS.—When progress had been re- ported upon the Corrupt Practices Bill at a quarter to seven o'clock on Tuesday evening, a large proportion of the mem- bers streamed out of the house unsuspieiously to dinner, be- lieving that there only remained the formality of moving the adjournment for the evening sitting. Before this motion had been moved. Mr. Warton unexpectedly meved a "count," in order to prevent the re-assembling of the House at night, but the attempt failed, as a more than sufficient number of members were hurriedly brought back, and the adjournment was then moved in due course.—Thnes.

At last we have it on irrefragable testimony, from Ogdens- burgh, that old Grimes's pulse has finally ceased to beat. A few mornings since, when the thermometer was nearly played out, a ragged little beggar stopped at the door of Judge J— and plaintively suggested food. The benevo- lent lUdy of the house engaged him in conversation: "What is your name' my boy ?" "My name is Grimes." Is your father living?" "Yes, marm." "I thought Old Grimes' was dead long ago." "That was my grandpa!" And the youngster waddled off, thinking what "a good old soul" the lady was.—Harper's Monthly. THE PARCELS POST.—The Gazette contains a copy of a Treasury warrant giving the text of the regulations with re- gard to the Parcels Post, which will come into operation on the Ist day of August next. The substance of the regula- tions has already been given. Parcels must not exceed 71b. in weight; they must be prepaid, the rate being 3(1. for lib., 6d. for 31b., 9d. for 51b., and is. for 71b.; they should not be posted on Sundays, Christmas Day, or Good Fliday ; and extra charge will be made for parcels "left till called for." No immoral work or explosive substance will be con- veyed, and each parcel can only contain goods for the per- son to whom it is addressed, and not for re-delivery to other persons. The Postmaster-General states that he is not re- sponsible for loss or damage.

A sad accident is reported from the vicinity of Stewarton, in Ayrshire. On Wednesday night about seven o'clock, while Mr. Robert Miller farmer, Wardlaw, his wife, three of their children, and a neighbour farmer named Robert Howie, were standing at the byre door looking at the peculiar ap- pearance of the sky they were struck by a flash of lightning, and knocked to the ground. Mrs. Miller was killed on the spot, and Mr. Miller is now supposed to be in a critical con- dition. Mr. Howie has a peculiar wound across the chest, but he was able to walk home, and he is not considered to be in danger. The three children are more or less injured, and two of them are confined to bed. Information was dis- patched to Stewarton, and medical assistance was imme- diately sent to the arm of Wardlaw. - COTTON .MILL DESTROYED BY FlRE.—What is known as the New Mill, belonging to the Brookbottom Cotton Spin— ning Company, Limited, Mossley, was completely burned to the ground on Wednesday. The ire broke out in connection with one of the spinning mules in the fifth storey about half-past five, just as the mill hands were ready for leav- ing their work. The mill was of modern construction, and was well built of stone. It was five stories high, with an attic equal almost to the other rooms, and it contained 14 pairs of mules with about 27,000 spindles. At the time the fire broke out there was an unusual large stock of cotton in the mill, and great efforts were put forth to get this oat, but a large portion was considerably ctamaged by water. The mill was insured in the offices of the Lancashire, Pbcenix' Royal, and the National of Ireland. The loss is estimated at upwards of £25,000. Two bunked hands were employed at the mill. -
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

CORRUPT PRA.CTICES BILL —Committee was resumed on the Corrupt Practices Bill. On clause 17, which gives the High Court or Election Court power to exempt an innocent act from being an illegal practice, Sir RICHARD CROSS moved to leave out "from inadvertence or from accidental miscalculation, or from other reasonable cause of a like nature," and insert "from some reasonable cause." The ATTORNEY. GENERAL opposed the amendment, which, after some discussion, was withdrawn. Some verbal amendrn ,nts having been made on the clause it was added to the Bill. On clause 18, relating to the nomination of an election agent, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL moved to insert as a new sub-section "that a candidate may name himself as an election agent, and thereupon shall, so , far as circumstances admit, be subject to the provisions of this Act both as a candidate and an election agent, and any reference in this Act to an election agent shall b 3 construed to refer to the candidate acting in his capacity of election agent." The amendment was agreed to, and the clause, as amended, was added to the Bill. Clause 19, 20, and 21 were added to the Bill. Clause 22, dealing with the payment of expenses through agents, was verb dly amendect and added to the Bill. On clause 23, which prescribes the period for sending in claims and making payments for election expenses, Sir RICHARD CROSS moved the omission of the words "dis- pensing with bill of particulars and receipts for sums under twenty shillings."—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL opposed the amendment, but consented to raise from twenty to forty shillings the maximum sum that should be exempt from re- ceipts, &c.—The latter proposal was agreed to.—Lord GEO. HAMILTON moved that an agent paving an account after the prescribed period, instead of being guilty of an illegal practice, should on summary conviction b 3 liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds. The AT- TORNEY-GENERAL thought he had Made provisions that would carry out the object of the amend- ment.—Mr. GIBSON thought it would be monstrous that a principal should be responsible for an agent's act that worked no corruption in paying a fair, though an il- legal, 'charge. and that a seat should by that act be ren- dered void.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said if the amend- ment was withdrawn, he would try to meet the difficulty by raising the maximum penalty or in some other way.—The amendment was withdrawn:—Mr. RYLANDS moved that the period for sending in claims be 14 days.—This was agreed to.—Lord R. Clinactrini, moved to,reduce the period for the examiaation of election accounts from 30 to 21 days.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL would accept 28, which was agreed to. Clause 23, as amended, was added to the Bill. HO USE OF LORDS--THURSDAY.

COUNSELLOR THEREFORE.—Another curious Beefstealcer, or member of the Beefsteak Club, was Serjeane Kelly, a celebrity of the Irish Bar. He had a remarkable habit of drawing conclusions directly at variance with his premises, and his nickname had consequently become "Counsellor Therefore." Curran described him as a perfect human per- sonification of a non sequitur. Meeting Curran one Sunday near St. Patrick's, he said to him, "The Archbishop's dis- course wassin excellent one this morning. It was well written andiVell delivered; therefore, I shall make a point of being at the Four Courts to-morrow at ten." At another time he met a friend, to whom he said, "What a delightful day for walking! therefore, I must go home and stop in- doors all day." In court, on one occasion, he said," The case is so clear, gentlemen, than you cannot possibly mis- understand it, and I should pay your understandings a very poor compliment if I dwelt upon it for another mieute; therefore, I shall at once proceed to explain it to yon as minutely as possible."—London Society. . MARRIAGE wine A DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER.—As a proof of the accuracy of the assertion of the Royal Com- missioners that these marriages are not dependent on legis- lation, Mr. Paynter Allen, secretary of the Marriage Law Reform Association, states that on Tuesday and Wednes- day he received nine new applications for information-as to the best means of contracting such a marriage in England or on the Continent. A working man, writing from Scot- land, says that he has waited for a change in the law for four years, and he will now go to Seitz eland. Another cer- respondent says that if the bill were delayed till 1885 there would be so many of these marriages in Ireland alone as will compel the Legislature to pass it. A third says that his family has belonged to the Church for 200 years, but since the recent vote of the bishops he hart joined the Non- conformists; and a fourth says that he intends to sell his business and go to Australia. This is the third case which ha e come to Mr. Allen's knowledge since Thursday of per- sons intending to quit England permanently in consequence of the rejection of the marriage bill. As UNLUCKY PUBLlCA.N.—Wilbrabam Cloug-11, landlord of the Engine Inn, Sewell-street, Prescot, was charged on Tuesday with supplying drink to a drunken man. It ap- peared-that about two weeks ago, two policemen found a man named Worrall, who was drunk, sitting in defendant's house with drink before him, having been supplied by defendant's daughter. The man was taken into custody and fined at a previous petty sessions. -- Defendant, for whom Mr. Swift appeared, denied that tile man was drunk, and a number of people living in Sewell-street, who had seen Worrall going along that street in the custody of the police, likewis averred that he was not drunk.—Defendant was fined 20s and costs, and the magistrates declined to tenew the provi- sional license under which he occupied the house.
