The following reply has been sent by the Town Clerk to Sir Henry Ponsonby:—"ln the absence of the Lord Provost, who has been in London for some days on public business, your telegram has been received. Please convey to the Queen deep and grateful appreciation of Her Majesty's kind enquiries. The number of persons who have lost their lives is still unknown. Fifty-two bodies have been recovered. Search is being actively prosecuted. Result will be telegraphed to you to-morrow morning. Her Majesty's kind expression of sympathy will be immediately communi- cated to the bereaved." Operations were on Thursday commenced by the Under- writers' Association for raising the Daphne, now lying sub- merged in the Clyde, but the appliances at command were found inadequate, and further efforts were postponed until the arrival of lifting pontoons and other apparatus. During the day a large number of funerals took place. Five men who were reported missing have been found alive and well, and thus to a slight extent the disaster is lessened, but all accounts agree that the death-roll will be close upon 150. At a meeting of the Glasgow Town Council, on Thursday, syntriathetic references were made to the calamity, and a telegram was sent to Her Majesty expressing grateful ap- preciation for her kindness in inquiring after the bereaved. Very few bodies were brought to the surface on Thursday, as the majority of the corpses lie in portions of the vessel to which the divers cannot penetrate without running grave flake.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

InOligence has reached Dublin that a farmer named Griller, residing at Morriss Mills, county Clare, was fired at on Wednesday night near kis own house and severely wounded. No cause can be assigned for theoutrage, and no arrests have been made up to the present. The Rev. Thomas Burke, the celebrated Dominican weacher and orator, died on Monday at his residence in the convent in Tallaght, near Dublin. He was the most dis- tinguished pulpit orator in the Roman Catholic Church in Ireland. _ _

In the Dublin Exchequer Division, on Saturday, a breach of promise case was heard before the Lord Chief Baron and a special city jury. Miss Margaret Coghlan was the plain- tiff, and Mr. Edward Spring the defendant. The damages were laid at £3,000, and the jury found a verdict for the plaintiff; damages, £1,200. An exhibition of Irish manufactures and works of art was opened at Cork on Tuesday. The "city bands" had refused to play in the procession because the promoters insisted on the National Anthem b2ing performed. The opening here- mony;in which Lord Bandon was the principal figure, passed off very successfully. "God save the Queen" was sung by a choir, and the large audience applauded heartily. At Dublin, on Saturday evening, Lord Wolseley was pre- sented with an address and service of plate at a banquet in the Rotunda. The Lord Lieutenant was present, and spoke hopefully of Ireland's position after her recent troubles. Responding to the toast of his health, Lord Wolseley said his countrymen required more scow for their talents than was afforded by their own island. He denied that his senti- ments were in any way anti-Irish, and declined to be dis- sociated from the gallant Irish soldiers, with whom he had spent so many years. On Monday the votes taken on Saturday in County Mona- ghan were counted, with the following result :—Mr. T. M. Healy (Nationalist), 2,376; Mr. 5: Monroe, Q.C. (Conserva- tive), 2,011; Mc. Pringle (Liberal), 274. Mr. Healy, ad- dressing the crowd subsequently, said that Ulster had, by that day's proceedings, flang herself into the arms of Ire- land and "hunted back" the candidate of that "proud Minister," Mr. Gladstone. He regarded his return as a de- mand for a speedy reform of the Land Act. Mr. Parnell also spoke. Gratifying tesiimony to the improved state of affairs in Ireland was given by Mr. Justice Murphy in his charge to the County Sligo grand jury on Wednesday. His Lordship said there was nothing whatever in the calendar to call for any notice from him, the cases being in the main of a trivial character. There was also a great decrease in the offences reported to the police. The number for the first half of 1882 was 135, while that for the past six months was only 18. The learned judge thought it was "quite probible" that the certainty of punishment following the commission of crime had had something to do with this improvement.

THE MINCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE. The Select Committee on the Manchester Ship Cana Bill gave their decision on the preamble on Wed- nesday. In giving the decision the Chairman said the Committee do net think it necessaty in consider- ing the question of the preamble to deal with the cases of the various petitioners who have come before us except those concerned in the estuary. The smaller matters—the Manchester Racecourse Company, Mr. Hargreaves, Sir H. De Trafford—although I do not say that his is a very small case—and the larger cases of the railway companies, all seem to the Committee to be matters of clauses. If these various interests go on, presuming that the promoters go on after they have heard the conditions the Committee con- sider necessary, then they will be matters for clauses. Per- haps some of those petitioners will reserve themselves, if the bill goes on, for the House of Lords, and then, I ouppose, we should not insert the clauses for them here. As condition precedent to the proof of the preamble, the promoters must insert in the bill the following provisos :- 1. The canal shall be devided into two sections, the lower section to include the works authorised in the hill below, and including Walton dock; the upper section to commence at Walton and include all works up to that point. 2. The company shall be restrained from proceeding with any of the works authorised by the bill unless, and until, they shall have obtained the necessary proviso to construct the estuary works. 3. The company shall apply to Parliament to sanction the details of any scheme on which they may have agreed with the Mersey conservators for the construction of the works in the estuary. 4. The company shall be restrained from proceeding with the upper section above Walton lock until the estuary works have been so far completed as to show to the satisfacti It of the Beard of Trade whether or not they, are likely to injure the estuary or the approaches thereto, and until a certificate shall have bsen obtained from the Board of Trade that in the opinion of that department and of the Mersey Conser- vators the works will not be injurious, and can lee pe-mitted to remain. This is what we indicated before, but we have inserted "the Board of Trade" with the Mersey Conservators, and left out the obligation to make a certain depth of water. 5. The company shall bind themselves to discontinue, alter, or remove, at their own cost, the said estuary works If directed to do so by the Mersey Conservators, and in such way as may be directed by them. 6. The company shall give such security as the Board of Trade may from time to time direct, to ensure the observance of the foregoing stipulations. 7. The company shall be restrained making the railway deviations No. 1 and N 0.2 until the above-mentioned certifi- cate as to the satisfactory nature of the works has been ob- tained from the Board of Trade. 8. The promoters must bring up a series of paragraphs to be added to the preamble, giving a history of the case as regards the estuary works and the bearing thereof on the other works. You will see (the Chairman added) that, generally speak- ing, the bill, bearing upon another bill that has to be after- wards passed, is irregularand should not be passed, but this is an anomalous case, and the preamble should therefore ex- plain by a proper recital what has led the Committee to pass an irregular hill. These paragraphs must of course be submitted to the Committee before they are brought up. The committee met again on Thursday. The first an- nouncement made was to the effect that the railway-com- panies and other opponents had withdrawn from furthee participation in the proceedings, and intended to reservr themselves for the contest before the House of Lords' Com- mittee. The "argued history" of the scheme was sub- mitted, and the committee took exception to a part which stated that the low-water channel was in their view " neces- sary and reasonably practicable." These words, it was urged, would hive made the channel "the child of Parlia- ment," and in lieu of them words were inserted declaring that the channel was "an integral po:tion of the scheme." An important conversation took place with regard to the clauses empowering municipal corporations and local boards lo subscribe towards the cost of the scheme. The committee, disregarding Mr. Pemlar's representations that the autho- rities mentioned were anxious to subscribe, struck the clauses out of the Bill. THE WARRINGTON CLAUSES. The Chairman then intimated that the committee would hear the arguments respecting the Warrington clauses, al- though they could not deal with them at that point of the case. Mr. Michael then read the agreement tvhich had been en- tered into between the promoters and the Corporation and mlnufacturess and traders of Warrington, and submitted that it was an equitable one, and that the clauses for carrying it out should be added to the Bill. Mr. Saunders., Q.C., who represented the traders of War- rington, was about to address the committee, when The Chairman said he did not think the learned counsel bade locus standi, as the traders had already come to an agreement with the promoters. Mr. Saunders said he would be perfectly content to leave the case of the traders in the hands of the promoters. Mr. Michael, Q.C., then read and explained the claims which it was proposed to put in to carry out the agreement arrived at between the promoters and the Corporation and traders of Warrington. Mr. O'Hara, on behalf of the Warrington Waterworks Company, objected to so much of the clauses as provided that in certain circumstances the promoters should supply water to the traders of Warrington for manufacturing pur- poses. He contended that the agreement between the pro- moters and the corporation ought not to be embodied in the Bill, but if it was thought necessary, to do the least that he could ask was that a saving clause should be inserted to pro- tect the interests of the water company, and to make it clear that no new rights, privileges, or powers in reference to the supply of water at Warrington were conferred by this Bill upon any person or company. Mr. Michael contended that the rights of the water com- pany would be in no wty invaded or prejudiced by includ- ing the agreement in the Bill. The water company, on the contrary, were attempting to set up a claim to monopoly which they did not legally possess. The traders on the banks of the river had an inherent right to take water from the river, and they were not bound to go to the waterworks company for a supply. Water companies were bound to supply water for domestic purposes, but they were not bound to supply water for trade purposes until the domestic sup- ply hsti been given. The promoters interfered with the rights of riparian proprietors, and in order to settle the op- position they undertook to give them compensation for the water abstracted for the canal. They were only taking pow era which were formerly exercised by the manufacturers, and without the agreement they could not do it. Mr. O'Hara said that if the promoters did not 'intend to do the waterworks company any harm they could not object to the clause he proposed. The Chairman: Does the Bill give the promoters any powers? Mr. Michael: Not any. - The Chairman: Then why not bind yourselves by agree- ment outside the Bill? Mr. O'Hara: That is what I should prefer. Mr. Michael submitted that it was a common practice to schedule agreements such as proposed by the pro- moters. After considerable conversation and a private consulta- tion, the Committee decided to insert a proviso that nothipg in the Act or the aereement set forth in the schedule should " KEATING'S POWDER?' MR. BRIGHT ON INDIAN BANKING.

Mr. John Bright appeared on Wednesday in the novel capacity of an advocate of a somewhat speculative enter- prise, but speculation of a kind that is only taken in hand by those who have the best interests of their fellow creatures at heart. The occasion was a meeting of the East Indian Association, to hear a paper read by Sir W. WedJerburn on -" The Poona Ryots Bank," and in a preliminary address, Mr. Bright spoke at length on the condition of the Indian agri- cultural population, and the means which were about to be proposed to contribute to their welfare. This is a matter in which the English public are more nearly concerned than is generally supposed. England's trade with India is very large,but both imports and exports would be indefluitely in- creased were the condition of the great mass of the Indian Ipeople improved. The demand for British manufactures would increase, further employment would be given to ship- ping, and British workmen would reap the benefit in brisker trade and the more liberal supply of Indian produce. But Mr. Bright showed that, as matters now stand in India. ma- terial progress is all but impossible. Oct of 100 people in India 80 depend upon the soil for existence, and out of every 100 who are thus agriculturists 80 depend upon borrowed motley, and of these about 50 are in so distress- ingly poor a donli Linn that they can only borrow on the most ruinous terms, interest being levied at rates varying from 12 to 30 per cant. Taking the rate of interest at mid- way between these figures—namely, 21 per cent.—it is obvious that no tillers of the soil who have to work with capital borrowed at this rate of interest can prosper, and the proposal advocated by Mr. Bright was the formation of banks or loan societies, which would advance working capital to these poor but industrious agriculturists at a reason- able rate of interest, and so afford them an opportunity to win prosperity, while at the same time the improvement that would thus be brought about in the condition of the people of India would strengthen the union between that great dependency and this country, and stimulate British trade and commerce. Tha need for such a movement as this i 3 obvious enough, and it is to be hoped that it can be placed upon a business footing that will ensure its success.

DEATH OF THE DUKE OF MARLBOROUGH. The Duke of Marlborough died very suddenly early on Thursday morning, at his residence, 29, Berkeley-square, Leyden, from an attack of cardiac syncope. His Grace is succeeded in the title by his eldest son, the Marquis of Blandford, who in politics is a Liberal. The last public ap- pearance of the noble duke was in the House of Lords, on Thursday week, when he moved the rejection of the Deceased Wife's Sister Rill. John Witi,ton Spencer-Churchill, K.G., seventh Duke of Marlborough, was born on June 2nd, 1822, ' and succeeded his father in 1357. The deceased nobleman sat as M.P. for Woodstock in the Conservative interest from 1844 to 1845, and again from 1847 to 1857. He was Lord Steward of tier Majesty's Household in 1866 67, Lord President of the Council in 1863, and Viceroy of Ireland from 1876 to 1880. He mar- ried in 1843 Lady Frances Anne Emily Vane, eldest daughter of the third Marquis of Londonderry. His grace leaves two sons and several daughters; the eldest of the family being the Mat-gals of Blandford, who succeeds to the dukedom, anfl who was born in May, 1844. The second son, Lord Randolph Churchill, M.P. for Woodstock, was born in. 1849. The late ' duke's eldest daughter is married to Lord Wimborne, and another is Duchess of Roar- burghe. George Charles Spencer-Churchill (Matquis of Blandford) was born May 14, 1844.; was educated at Eton, and was formerly Lieutenant in the Royal Horse Guards, and Captain in the Oxfordshire Yeomanry Cavalry; he is a J.P. for Oxfordshire, and was married in 1869 to Lady ',Alberta Frances Anne Hamilton, daughter of the let Duke of Abercorn. KG., and has issue Charles Richard John (Earl of Sunderland), born 1871; Lady Prances Louisa, horn 1873; and Lady Lilian Maud and Lady Nora Beatrice liar- , riette, born 1875. The Marquis, who was divorced from , his wife a few months ago under painful circumstances, will ; become the patron of thirteen livings.

div.head: BANQUET TO, LORD EGERMN OF
div.p: BANQUET TO, LORD EGERMN OF
TATION.

A. banquet was given.on.Wednesday evenings. at the Mar- ket Hall, Knutsford, to Lord Eaerton of Tatton, in recogni- tion Of his lordship's long services as one of the members for the county. There were about a hundred ladies and gentlemen present. Mr. T. W. Tatton, of Wythenshawe, occupied the chair, and amongst the company were Lady Egerton of Tattoo, Mr. Allan de Tatton Egerton, M.P. and Mrs. Allan Egerton, Mr. Cunlifte Brooks, M.P., Sir R. Brooke and Lady Brooke, and: Sir Philip and Lady Main- war ing. The toast of the evening," The health of Lord: Egerton of Tatton," was proposed by Mr. W. IL Houldsworth, the Conservative candidate for Manchester, who spoke of Lord Egerton's long parliamentary services. It was just a quarter of a century since his lordship, then the Hon. Wil- braham Egerton, was elected for North Cheshire, and be was electedin 1868, 1874, and 1880 as one of the members for Mid-Cheshire. Not only as a member of the House of Commons, but as a county geutleman, his lordship's work had been of the most useful character. Lord Egerton, in replying, was received with loud cheers. He said he could not adequately thank then, for their kind- ness during the time he had sat in the House of•Cornmons ; twenty-livo years an he was and in that accession, when selected a young and untried man, to enter Parliament, he felt that this was dooe on the strength of the long services of his father. (Cheers). During his career he had • en- deavoured to follow his father's example and to do his dirty. It was with some pride and.satisfactien than he recollected that for over fifty years he and his father had represented divisions of that county. (Hear, hear ) Ile trusted that he left the torch of Conservatism burnieg, as biightly as he found it (Cheers). Mr. Disraeli, speaking an Manchester on our constitutional system, said it woeld be et great mis- take to suppose that the House of Lords was nut in its way as representative as the House of Ca.ninons. (Hear, hear.) He was happy to be able to claim it tn he so, for ea long as he had health and strength he should endeavoer te do his duty to his old constitutents as their representative in the Upper Chamber. (Cheers.) Althou4h be was removed from active association with many old friends in the House of Commons, he felt that he had as usetul a sphere of duty before him as ever he had. (Hear, hear.) He could not agree with the remark of Mr. Chamberlain that the class to which Lord Salisbury belonged was a class that "toiled not neither did they spin." He could not but remember that the character and glory of the country were in old days founded and raised by the gentty, and the nobility was quite as honourable as to have been successful in trade. (Cheers.) He was quite aware of the services which com- merce and trade had rendered to this cournry, and he should be the last to speak disparagingly of therli. He only claimed for the class he represented an equal share in the work and government of the eountry. (Cheers.) There had been a considerable change in the character of the House of Commons during the last twenty-five years. It was difficult to say what the causes of this change were. Some persons attributed it to the extension of the suffrage, but in the first Parliament, when Lord Beaconsfield and Sir Stafford Northcote led the House, there was not the altera- tion in the character of the House that was now seen. When he entered Parliament there were only two parties, and there was an honourable understanding between them so as to facilitate the Progress of business; but new there were four distinct parties not counting what was c riled the Fourth Party. He didn't believe what was called the Fourth Party was a party in itsetf. Its members were loyal Conserva- tives, who took the Liberal view of their powers of aggres- sion. (Laughter and cheers), They had the Liberal party, the Radicals—Who were for im- proving our institutions off the face of the earth—the Irish party and the Conservatives. One cause of the present order of things was that the leader of the House had not led well. The Geyernizient had been a vacil- lating Government, and the consciences was that the house appeared to be entirely beyond his centrol. For a remedy for the present difficulties and evils in the House of Com- mons, he thought they must look to the constituence.s, who must be shown that the Government sent in 1880 had been a mistake, that they had done nothing but commit blundere. He was hopeful of the prospects of the Conservative party, and as long as he -was able he should take the same interest as he had always done in the welfare and advancement of the Conservative cause. (Cheers.) Mr. T. Nash proposed "The House of Lords," which was responded to by Mr. W. Cunliffe Brooks, M.P.; and other toasts followed.

BRIGADE DRILL OF VOLUNTEERS AT NEWTON COMMON. In brilliant weather and in the presence of a large con- course of spectators the 2nd Lancashire Engineer Volunteers (St. Helens) ; the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers (War- rington); and 21st Lancashire Rifle Volunteers (St. Helens) were put through brigade drill by Colonel Harry Bell, on Saturday afternoon last, on Newton Common—a site which is excellently situated and most admirably adapted for the purpose. Colonel Bell, who is the officer commanding the Bth and 40th regimental districts (Liverpool and Warring- ton) organised a series of brigade drills for the instruction of the volunteers under his command, and this was the fifth of the series, the former drills having been held in Sefton Park, Liverpool. Under the new territorial scheme the 9th and 21st L.R.V. are respectively called the Ist and 2nd Volunteer Battalions of the South Lancashire Regiment (Prince of )Vales's Own Volunteers), and as Saturday last was the first occasion upon which they had been bri- gaded together under their new relations, all the more in- terest was centred in the event. The corps were drawn up in the centre of the Common the spectators numbering several thousands, being kept back by 70 man of the Newton detachment of the 19th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers (Liver- pool Press Guard), under the command of Captain J. 14 Wood. The latter assembled at the storehouse at Newton about four o'clock, and on arriving at the Common, a line of sentries was formed in a vast square, while Captain Wood, with commendable foresight, established a line of !leg eig- nallers from Earlestown station to the Common, and by that • means the arrival of Colonel Bell at the station was instantly signalled. The whore of the men wero drawn up in line of quarter-columns to receive the Brigadier; the Engineers being on the left, the 21st Rifles in the centre, and the 9th Rifles on the right. The former were under the command of Lieutenant Colonel .1. Bothwell, the other officers present being Major Wilcock, Capt. and Adjutant Currie, Captains S. Craike and Duffy, Lieutenants Sloncrief, Perullebury, Mc- Kechnie, Lyon, and Bothwell. The strength of the regi- ment was 9 officers. 23 sergeants, 34 bandsmen, and 208 sappers, total 279 of all ranks. Major R. Pilkinc,ton was in command of the 21st Rifle Volunteers, an a there were also present Major and Adjutant Wilcock, Major Bramwell, Major Windus, Major White, Captains Brown, Waring, Brunner, Lieutenants J. C, Uramble, B. Gamble, Janson, Neil, Dickinson, Sayers, Hadley, and Parr; the remaining strength being 24 sergeants, 40 bandsmen, and 370 men; total 450. The Warrington contingent—the 9th Lencashire Rifle Volunteers—was commanded by Colonel Greenall, Captain and Adjutant O'Leary, Captains Bol- ton, Litton, Ridgway, Heptierd, and Widdows, Lieutenants Thompson and Gooch. T,lere were nine officers, 21 corporals, 40 bandsmen, and 370 men, altogether a total of 440. Thus there was a total strength of 1,169 men of all ranks. Colonel Bell was accompanied by his Brigade Major, and Captain A. D. Seton, of the Bth L.A.V., as aide-de-camp, and at ten minutes to six his arrival at Earleetown statien was signalled to the officers on the Com- mon. Punctually at the time announced—six o'clock—he made his appearance, and, as he approached., the men pre- sented arms. The three bands massed together near the saluting point and struck up an appropsiate air as the whole of the men were drawn up for a march past in double companies. Tne bright scarlet uniforms of the Engineers and the 9th Rifles formed a striking contrast to the dark green and sombre-looking attire of the men of the 21st, while the glittering arms, the music of the bends, and the Union Jack flowing in the gentle breeze, were all conducive to making the scans a thoroughly martial one. As the men marched past in splendid array the spectators warmly applauded them—a compliment which was well sleseeved. On return- ing in quarter-column formation they excellently acquitted themselves, and also in the march past in line battalions. Other movements were afterwards carried out—and though some of the evolutions were not marked with Out skill and finish which is observable among the "Regulars," there was still sufficient to show that the volunteers as a whole are a smart body of men, and competent to fulfil the duties they are expected to perform. The drill occupied about two hours, and at the close the men were drawn up on three sides of a square. Colonel Bell, addres- sing the men, said be was sure they would all agree with him after the experience they had had of the last two hours that a little brigade drill would do them no harm. He was glad indeed to have had the opportunity of meeting them, and considering the little practice they got of such drills he must congratulate them all upon having done so well. But at the same time they must see there were deficiencies and no one could exPect them to do the drill properly un- less they had practice. He was sure they would all under- stand and see the great advantage there was to be obtained in coming out into the rlpen with other troops. There was no doubt about it that the knowledge of a few brigade dale was of more use to them than a dozen battalion drills in their own drill-shed. As they had had that meeting once he hoped to have it again. Whenever any of the commanding officers thought they could got their rev. ments together, and would only drop him a line, he would be very glad indeed to make arrangements and do every- thing he could to encourage the volunteer serviee. Be thought it would be of much advantage if they had a! little more of such brigade exercises. They might think etlead been uninteresting that day, but it bad been of gl,at:Ctse. They had only been able to do the rucliru three ents aOV-er-d show how they got or;, tv* i, but if they r even- ings they could get on to mhuacbn'olo or re advanced systems of drill. As they had got a long way to go back be would not detain them any longer, but wish them all good even- ins (Applaurse.)—The men of the various battalions then tea. up different positions in the field, and refreshment, in the shape of pork pies, beer, gingerbeer, &c,', were distribu- ted. The SL Helens companies afterwards marched to Collins Green station, while the 9th L.B.V. proceeded to Earlestown station (their passage through the town being viewed with interest by a large number of persons) and left there shortl' before ten o'clock. In every respect the meeting !as an encouraging success, though ecarcely as many wren put man appearance as was generallyanticipatede

SATURDAY, JULY 7, 1883.

THE County Monaghan election has re- sulted in the return of Mr. HEALY, the Nationalist candidate, and this result is mainly noteworthy as being the first success Mr. PARNELL has achieved in the Province of Ulster, long considered the hotted of Con- servatism. For some time, however, there have been evidences of a change setting in, i and n no constituency in the Province waS this more apparent than in County Monaghan, political opinion in which appears to have undergone more than one transformation, During the past low years this change has been more especially marked. From 1832--- the year in which the first Reform Bill waS passed—to 1852 the representation of the constituency was divided, a Liberal and a Conservative being returned at each succes- sive election; but in the last-mentioned year an alteration—though it is not quite apparent why—was effected, and, except during one brief interval, the constituency was thence- forward represented by two ConservativeS until the last general election, when two Liberals took their place. The interval re- ferred to extended from 1865 to 1868, during which period one of the seats was held bY Lord CREMORNE, a Whig. The contests which have taken place in the constituencY would seem to indicate rapid strides have been made in advanced views; but we are disposed to question whether the allegiance to Mr. HEALY will be of a permanent charac- ter. The late Mr. isAAc Burr contested the county in 1871 against Mr. (now Sir) T. LES- LIE, but the former was defeated by a veil large majority, the numbers being LESLIE/ 2,521; BUTT, 1,528 Mr. BUTT, therefore, was in a minority of 993. The Horne Rulers contested the representation again 111 18741 and though their position had many festly improved, still they were so far re- moved from victory that they did not think worth while to dispute the Conservative posr tion in 1880. In this year, however, the Liberals offered opposition, and the Conser' vatives were then, for the first time since the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, entirelY deprived of any share in the representation: Messrs. GIVAN and FINDLATER, two excellenfr Liberals, being elected by considerabie majorities. The numbers on this occasion were—GrvAN (L), 2,239 FINDLATER c.,l))t z,coB ; LESLIE (C), 1,734; and SHIRLEY 1,664. The vacancy which has just be filled was caused by the resignation or Alf: GTVAN, who has been appointed Crown Soil, citor for the counties of Meath and Kildare..., and the opportunity was seized by the aci,t vanced section of the Irish party to again their strength in the constituency. der HEALY resigned his seat for Wexford in or,i to do battle for his leader and his cause, if we except a few characteristic express to which he gave utterance, and which refiCC4

tinue, alter, or remove, at their own cost, the said estuary works if directed to do so Mersey Conservators, and in such way as may be directed by them." The remaining conditions are comparatively unimportant. It will thus. be seen that before a shovel or spade can be used the promoters must agree with the Mersey Conservators, then obtain a Bill, next confine their operations only to the estuary of the Mersey, and probably after- wards find—which we sincerely hope may not be the case if they should go on with the works—that all the time, the labour, and the money spent, is to be unproductive. The prospect is certainly not a very bright one for investors, and there is no disguising the fact that with such strict provisions there will be more difficulty than was at one time supposed in raising the necessary capital. The possi- bility of any return for money that may be risked upon the undertaking—desirable as it undoubtedly is—is too remote to ensure the coffers of the promoters being replenished speedily. The Committee, on Thursday, 'in- serted in the preamble a declarati= to the effect that it appeared from the evidence that if th.e scheme could be carried out with due regard to existing interests the canal would afford valuable facilities to the trade of Lan- cashire, and ought to be sanctioned A declaration such as this coining from the Committee, who have spent so much time in investigating the merits of the scheme, mast, of course, have its weight with investors, and it will go a long way towards assisting the promoters to get their second Bill when thq ask for it ; still, we do not believe it is sufficent,to inspire capitalists with that confidence which they re- quire. If the present Bill passes the House of Lords, and a second Bill is obtained another year, and if excavations should .be commenced, it seems to 'us that Warrington will benefit lo some extent while these exca- vations last; it is now quite another question how far the canal will be advantageous to Warrington in the feture. The discussion which took place at the Council meeting, on Tuesday, with.respect to the clauses to be in- serted in the Bill for the benefit of the traders cot- Warrington discloses a phase of this 'ques- tion Which it was /lever contemplated would arise. It is clear 'by that agreement that the present traders and their. successers are secured ; it appears, however, to be doubtful howlar future traders will be allowed to par- ticiple with the present traders in the privi- leges which be latter are to enjoy, and so long as there, exists any doubt upon this point it cannot ftil to deter manufacturers . from coming here, building works, and-so increas- ing the trae of the town and neighbourhood. We hope, however, that tire clauses are suffi- oiently comprehensive to enable—as they cer- tainly ought—not only the present' traders and their successors, but all fnture -traders to enjoy 11 the . water and other privileges just -'secured; if they do not, then it is well that the fears which exist in this regaid should be Iventilated, so that if possible a 7Temedy may I be applied.

; BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY, RUNCORN.— We would reglincl Our readers that the annual school ser- mons will be preached .at St, Patll't! ?Web tO-11101low (Sunday) by the-Rev. R._?. Downs, who is an eloquent and impressive preacher. THE INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES OF WIDNES have formed a new tent, which bears the name of the "Hope of Widnes." Bro. nomas Ray is chief ruler; Bro. Jos. Taylor, treasurer; and Bro. Macbeth, secretary. The society is registered under the new Friendly Sicieties' Act, aril offers great advantages to teetotallers. WIDNES POLICE Couu-r.—Yesterday, before Mr. Brock, Nicholas Brosvn anl Michael McEvoy, aged respectively 12 and 8 years, were charged with sleeping in an out-housc in Bedford-street,Lugsdale,on the previous night. The case was proved by P.C. Noble, and the prisoners were discharged with a caution.—John Gillespie, a tramp, *as charged with slef!ning in the same building, and he was committed to gaol for seven days. P.Q, Thouipstiti proved the case. RutVogtt PIC-NiC.—From our advertising Colritnas it will be seen that the members Pf the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association will hold their 'annual pic-nic on Saturday next, when a covered boat will go to Weaverham Wood along the Weaver Canal. The sail will be a most enjoyable one, winding as the canal does through a picturesque piece of country, while at the wood there are numerous objects of interest, including the *Relent chnrch. Tea will be provided. THE ST. HELENS CASUAL %Vital) COESTION.—The qies- tion of providing a casual ward in the borough of St. Helens seems for the past few months to havebeen held in abeyance,tho Guardians of the Prescot Union being reluctant to provide such an accommodation in St. Helens. The Corporation, who made a decided representation to the Guardians that such a ward should be provided, have not, it appears, alto- gether postponed thequestion, and it is probable that some- thing further will be heard upon the subject before another winter sets in. _ _ _ _ _ _

S PI RATO RS. ARREST OF GARRITTY

Rarnett or Bernard Garritty, who, as previ:m.siv stated in Tide ExantineP, lodged with Rogerson at Mrs. Coldron's, , Moss Bank, Widnes, and left the town abput two months ago. has been arrested by Sergeant O'Brien at Sln.lll•Ad. On leaving Widnes, the Dublin detective, from infotmation in his possfs3ion, went to Hu!dcrsfield, where he believed Garri: ty had taken refuge. Ile was not, however, successful in his search, but was lead to make enquiries at Sheffield which termirateil in the arrest of Garritty, who about six weeks ago found employment at same nurseries at Hands- worth, a few miles from Sheffield. On Thursday afternoon the village was visited by Sergeant O'Brien, who is stationed near Roscommon, accompanied by a Dublin detective and one from Manchester. On making their way to the nurseries Garritty saw O'Brien and recognised him. He thereupon started off and ran at the top off his speed, followed ty O'Brien and the other officers. The Pace Was kept up for some time, and uttimat,l34 Garritty was caught in a wood. The ii,Afiaiai charged him with blowing up some farm buildings in the neighbourhood of Roscommon wilt dyna- mite, but it is believed he is wanted for a much more serious charge. Upon this the officers were reticent. Much ex- citement followed the intelligence of the arrest, for many Irishmen are engaged at the nurseries. For fear of an at- tempt to rescue, Garritty was brought to Sheffield by a by- way and not by rOad. He will be taken to Dublin.

The trial of four prisoners charged with conspiracy to blow up with dynamite the residence of Mr. Muson, land agent, was resumed at Sligo yesterday. Evidence corroboratir;g that of Jones, an informer, having been given, Bryan Gerarty, another informer, who was recently arrested at Widnes-lane, was examined. He fully identified all prisoners and others who had absconded as having plotted the outrtge, and said Tansey, one of the prisoners, had declared they would be paid £5O if Weston House were blown up, and more if life were taken. Evi- dence in support of an alibi was then given for the defence, and the Court adjourned.

A WARNING TO ZUNCORN BOATMA.N.—At Runcorn -I; etty Sessions, on Monday, John Lawson, a boatman, was sum- :awned to answer a claim of £6 103. damages for haying 'neglected and refused to perform a contract of service which he had entered into with Messrs. Simpson, Davies and Sens, oeelauncorn.—Mr. Burton who represented the complein- man said the defendant 'had receetly been a boatman an , their employ, and proceedings were takeg against him under the Employers and Workmen's Act of 1875. The defendant had teen in Messrs. Simpson's employ some years, and it::, was his duty to obey the lawful commands of his masters.: 511 was arranged that their engagement should be terminated at a trin's notice on either side. On the 22nd ult. the de- fendant arranged to load a cargo for Wolverhampton, and on the nal the cargo was on board. He then proceeded to Messrs. Simpson's office, and from the cashier obtained £4 Se.on oaf etch? :sintopfl af rieniagnhtts to advance . aTkearec we thisa s nm osu h obligationte on the part defen- dant was not entitled to anything: but in order that be might have no austification for refusal they advanced him the money, it being distinctly understood that he should I Leave Runcorn on the Monday. On that day, apd also on the , Taesday, although frequently requested to proceed on the ' journey, be refused until he had received some more mosey on account of the freight. The owners on principle refused this demand, ad the boat lay idle at Runcorn until Thursday morning, when the defendant was discharged and another man put on board the boat. Mr. Burton stated that the prisoner ought to have been in a position to proceed with the boat at once without having a further advance of money, because during the seven weeks previous he had received no less a sum than £2l. As Messrs. Simpson and Davies employed a large number of men, they could not, of course, carry on their business if suele conduct as the defen• dent had been guilty of was tolerated. The claim was for 1.4 ss, for money advanced and three days demurrage at 15s. per dayi—Evidence bearing out this statement having been given by James Higgins and James Kent, the Bench made an order tor the payment ot the money by the defendant in three weeks.

CRIMINAL ASSAULT ON A GIRL AT RUNCORN, • Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. Cbtd- wick, a young man named Thomas Ball, living at Wand's- row, Halton-read, was charged with criminally assaulting Elizabeth Doyle, a girl 12 years of age.--The prosecutrix is the daughter of a blacksmith, who resides at 14, Brunswick-street, and on the 21th ult., whilst her parents were away, and she was engaged nursir g the baby, the prisoner went into the house for the purpose, he stated, of seeing how Hannah Jones was. At that time a woman called Maggie Jones Was present, but subsequently sha left; and the prisoner, who had been asleep on the sofa, got up, and took the baby from the prosecutrix's arms. He then threw her to the ground, and attempted to assault her. Infortnation was given to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended under a warrant.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday.

div.head: BOARD AND WATERLOO ROUSE.
div.p: THE BOARD AND WATERLOO ROUSE.

The following resolution was passed, on the motion of Rev. FATHER FENNELLY, seconded by Mr. LEA :—" The School Board will be willing to take the three last appor- tioned rooms at Waterloo House, subject to the settlement of the question by their solicitor as regards yearly rent and a lease upon the following terms: That no rent shall be com- menced before the Ist January, 1888; that the rent from the let January, 1888 shall be at the rate of £35 per annum, to include cleaning, lighting, heating, as well as all charges for water rates, and taxes; and that from the date of the re- , moval of the. School Board to Waterloo House until Decem- ber 3184 1887, the Improvement Commissioners shall under- take to ply all taxes and provide gas, water, and cleaning , materials for the yearly sum of £l5; that the Improvement Commissioners will undertake to put the offices in proper tepantable order,as well as make all requisite structural al t dra- dons as to doors, ttc., and to provide and fix not less than tin ee large cupboards to hold the papers of the School Boatel, and that as regards painting and papering the School Board shall be put to no expense, and the Commissioners shall carry out the work to the satisfaction of the School Board." —The CLERK was instructed to forward the resolution to the Board of Commissioners.

div.head: INTELIESTING STATISTICS.
div.p: INTELIESTING STATISTICS.

The visitor (Mr. Bowyer) presented his monthly report as follows:—Return from the 'Public Elementary Schools for June, 1883: Certified Government accommodation, 2716; total number on the rolls, 3,016; number on the rolls cor- responding period of last year, 2,849; increase in the number on the rolls, 167; total average attendance, 2,323 5 ; average attendance corresponding period of last ye tr, 2,121 8; per- centage of attendances, 77; average attendance for the year 1874, 1 2:52 ; increase in average attendance, as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 1,0715; accommodation in excess of average attendance, 392 5; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 300; number in attendance at Private Adventure Schools under fld per week, 62. The returns for the five weeks end- ing June 29th show a marked improvement in the attend- ance at the various schools. You will also notice that at four schools out of the 12 the average attendance has ex- ceeded the accommodation. There is now only accommoda- tion for girls at the Wesleyan School, the National, Trinity, Catholic, and Mill Brow Board school being practically full. According to the average attendance for the past month there is now only accommodation for 75 more girls. At the Attendance Committee meeting, held on the 20th June, I summoned 33 of the most neglectful parents to ap- pear before the committee. In 30 cases the notices were complied with. Only three failed to appear. Two cases were ordered to be dealt with under the bye-laws, and the remaining cases adjourned for a fortnight, to be further dealt with by the Board.

THE 'MARRIAGE OF CAPTAIN HAZLE- HURST, OF RUNCORN. WORKPEOPLE'S PARTY. To commemorate the marriage of Captain Hailehurst, J.P., of The Grange, Runcorn, to Miss Keen, of Edgbaston, Birmingham, which took place on the Tuesday previous, the workpeople of Messrs. Hazlehurst and eon, with their sweethearts and wives, were entertained to an excellent knife and fork tea in the Public Hall on Saturday after- noon. The building had been decorated for the occasion, and artistic scrolls bearing the words "Gad bless the bride and bridegroom" and "Good wishes for the bride and bridegroom" occupied prominent positions. The proceed- ings, which were thoroughly successful, were opened by Mr. J. H. Salkeld delivering a short address on behalf of the rm. He said he was pleased to see that so many persons had responded to the invitation to be present, and he bade 'them a hearty welcome. He hoped they would succeed in enjoying themselves, for that was the chief wish of the gen- tlemen whom they were met to honour. Captain littee-1 hurst had addreesed the following letter to him, which he had much pleasure in reading :—" Hotel, Belle Vue, Brussels, June 29th, 1883.—Dear Sir,--I hope you will all have an enjoyable evening on Saturday. Please express my thanks to the employes for their handsome present, anl tell them that I shall always prize it as a -souvenir of the gool feeling which always has existed, and I hope always will exist betwaeo my trill and our workpeople. I must appeal to them all toscontinue in the same coarse, and I would remind them that we are all dependent open each other for , the satisfactorvicsnduct of the business, and I hope that all, from the lads to the foremen, will de their best in the future as in the past. Again thanking them far their handsome gift." The reading of this communication was received with demonstrations of satisfaction by the 363 guests who 3 had assembled. Messrs. S tlkeld, S. Pope, R. Foalkes, J. Humphreys, W. Hough, Peter Davies, Mr. and Mrs. J. Hula ford, Mr. Jonathan Horsefield, and others occupied seats on the platform. The caterer was Mr. 11. Jackson, of Wilson's Hotel, and after tea Mr. W. H. Middleton's concert compeny gave an excellent entertainun tit, which concluded with three cheers for the -bride and bridevroom.—On Saturday else, Mr. A Keen the f ither of the bride, who ie managing dictator lof the Keen, Nut and Bolt Company, Birmingham, gave 1 the workmen and their wives, numbering in all about 2,400 persons, an excursion to Suttcn Park, where they were entertained to dinner. Five trains were required for the conveyance of the party to their destinatio.), but the arrangements were carried out satisfacterily, the trains arriving safely at Sutton about half-past 19. The party was accompanied by Mr. and Mrs. Keen and family, Mrs. Hazlehurse (mother of Capt. Elazlehurst), Mrs. Stevens (Mayoress of Bristol). Messrs. E. J. Grice (a managing 1 director), It. Howson, W. F. Jones (eecretary), J. Stevens (Bristol), tke. The,patk was looking its best, and the ex- cursionists fully enjoyed themselves, a great variety of amusements being provided in the grounds. Dinner was I served at thee Crystal Palace grounds, ample provision hav- ing been made to satisfy the wants of so large a number. After the repast various toasts were proposed and enthu- siastically honoured, amongst them being the health of the bride and bridegroom (prodosed by Mr. W. F—jones, and responded to by Mr. Keen); "Prosperity to the Patent Nut and Bolt Company;" and " rhe heath of Mr. and Mrs. Keen and family." The emplare:s of the Patent Nat and Bolt Company, Limited, of which the bride's father is managing director, were evetertained to dinner at the Crystal Palace, Sutton Coldfield, Birmingham, on Saturday. The emeloyes of the company front ,the London works, Smethwick, and Stour Valley Works, Weet-Brornwich, to the number of 2,400, were conveyed to Sutton Coldfield by special trains, the occasion being treated ae a general holiday. Dinner was provided in the large pavilion., and amongst those present were Messrs. Arthur Keen, It. Howson, E. J. Once (managing directors), B. J. ,Cereton (manager of the London works, Smethwick), Scattergood (manager of the Stour Valley works, West Bromwich), W. F, Jones ksecretary), W. B. Stevens (Bristol), the Mayoress of Bristol, Mrs. Stevens, Mrs, A. Keen, Mrs. C. Hszlehnrst (Halton Grange), the Misses Keen, dtc. At the conclusion of the dinner an apology Ifor non-attendance was announced from ttte chair- man of the company, Mr. J. D. Weston, (Mayor of Bristol.)—Mr. W. F. JONES, in proposine the thealth of the newly married couple, Captain and Mrs. C. W. Hazlehurst , said the match was in every respect a most agreeable one. The parties were highly respected, and arid their positions in life were tqual. (Applause.) The uraion that day, he hoped, would augur well for the future happiness of all concerned. It was the first occasion on which the employees of the Patent Net and Bolt Company, at London Works and the Stour Valley Works, had been united together for one common object, and out of respect to Mr...and Mrs. Keen, the parents of the bride. (Applause.) —Mr. eetRTRIJR KEEN, in responding to the toast, on behalf of Captain and Mrs. Hazlehurst, expressed regret at the un- avoidable absence of Mr. Weston, the chairman of the cone- piny. He thanked the employees most sincerely for the many expressions of goodwill towards himself and his family. He should never forget their kindness during the whole coneese of his life. (Applause.)—Mr. SCATTER- Go)D proposed "Prosperity to the Patent Nut and Bolt Company, Limited," a company which had, be said, Male 3,500 employees, and upon the prosperity of which 12,000 people depended for their daily bread. The name of the company was as well known in ,ite,ly as in England, and the same remark would apply to France, Russia, .Germany, and the other countries of Europe and America. The company had supplied the fastenings that had laid down nearly all the railways in the world, and if they ac a company ceased to exist there was no one who could take their place. He did not think there was asy staff that worked harder than the staff of the retent ifut and Bolt Company, nor was there a body of men connected with any institution in Great Britain that could equal theirs. (Applause.) He (Mr. Scattergood) had been connected with the company 20 years, and he could honestii may there was no one on the staff who worked harder than Hr. Keen. If the men continued to work as Mr. Keen worked, the further prosperity of the company would he assured. (Applause.)—Mr. A. KEEN, in acknow- ledging the compliment, said he had always felt proud of his employees, both before and since the amalgamation of his fir.n with the Patent Nut and Bolt Company.—Mr. SearrEnGoon also gave the health of Mrs. Keen, which was responded to by Mr. Keen.—During the proceedings, hearty cheers were given for Mr. and Mrs. Haeehurst, the chairman of the company, and the directors.—The party returned to their hones in the evening, having spent tie enjoyable day in the Eaton Park and Crystal Palau Liardens.

div.p: LATEST NE %VS.

The Canadian Fenian s are keeping a sharp look out for James Carey's arrival. At the meeting of the Council of the Royal Society, on Thursday, Professor Huxley was chosen president in place of the late Mr. Spottiswoode. . . .
Corporal Samuel Fawkner was leaning out of a window of the barracks at the Tower of London, on Thursday night, when be overbalanced himself, fell out, and was killed.

_ A sham fight took place at Alders-hot early yesterday morning, in the vicinity of Cm3ars Camp, when the Duke of Connaught successfully defended the camp against a superior attacking force under Major-General Willis.

div.p: THE CHOLERA IN EGYPT.
During the twenty-four hours ending at 9 p.m. on Thurs- day thete were 109 deaths from cbolera at Damietta and 68 at Mansnrah.
-TilE GREAT STRIKE OF IRONWORKERS.

Yesterday morning the whole of the ironworks in Wed- nesbury, Tipton, West Bromwich, and the .adjoining dis- tricts, were standing, and it is estimated that 30,000 men are out on strike. The rioters have done great damage to property, the loss in some instances being as much as £l,OOO. The conduct of the men is strongly condemned by the leaders.

div.head: ACTION AGAINST "GENERAL" BOOTH.
div.p: THE ACTION AGAINST "GENERAL" BOOTH.

Justice Stephen gave judgment yesterday in the case of Ebbetts v.. Booth, in which it was sought to obtain from "General" Booth the Grecian Theatre and Eagle Tavern, London, on the ground of breach of contract. His lordship pronounced that the covenants had been broken by the dis- turbances which naturally resulted from the processions of the Salvation Army, by the noisy way in which the services were conducted, and by the carrying on of the Eagle as a temperance hotel. Notice of appeal was given.
CAREER "OF AN INCCOVFDEIstRIOYisis.EXTRAORDINARY

A prisoner, named Jens Nielson, who on Sunday and Monday last set fire to five farmhouses near Copenhagen, has confessed that in February 1881, he caused the terrible fire in the Victoria Docks, with the object of obtaining plunder. He 'only found, however, three dresses and tw3 bonnets. Two days afterwards he set fire to a warehouse near London Bridge. On the same afternoon be was arres- ted for stealing, and the next day was sentenced at Bow- street to two months' imprisonment.

THE DYNAMITE SEIZURE IN BIRMINGHAM.
EXCRAORDINARY REQUEST BY THE CONVICT
WHITEHEAD,

Tbe convict Whitehead has made a remarkable request j to the Birmingham police authorities. Within the last few days a letter was received from him from the copvict prison where he is undergoing his sentence of penal servitude for life asking that his personal effects" should be sold and the money distributed among his friends in- America. . His "personal effects" may be summed up as the carboys ef acid, the bottles of,glycerine,ind the paper and paint seized at his pretnivs in Ledsam-street. Altogether, the value of 'these goods in their original state would be £3O to £4O, but -sane of the acid has been so "manipulated" by Whitehead as to be practically useless. This stuff having been tested by a practical chemist and pronounced useless, the police have ordered it to be destroyed. The pure acid clmmanded a ready customer in a well-known Birmingham manufac- turer, and it is believed the proceeds will beat once remitted to Whitehead. It was specially stipulated that the put- chaser should remove the wicker-work from the carboys be- fore allowing them to leave his premises, so as to guard against the possibility of any of the nitro-glycnine clinging to it. The task of disposing of the bottles of glycerine was not sueh an easy matter. No amount of persuasiveness on the part of the amateur auctioneer, a detective it is under- stood, would induce anyone to purchase the glycerine, though it was pronounced thoroughly pure, and the same uncompromising prejudice was manifested to- wards the paints and paper which were found in the dynamite laboratory in Ledsam-street. The. glycerine, therefore, remains unsold up to the present. As regards the paints and paper, as they are of greater value than a few shillings, it will be a matter of grave concern to White- head's "friends" if they remain unsold. It is amusing to I note Ike strong objection which is generally entertained to- wards the glycerine, notwithstanding that its perfect purity and harmlessness can be guaranteed. The explanation is said to be that tradesmen are naturally afraid of its becom- ing known that they have some of Whitehead's glycerine in their premises. It may be mentioned that Whitehead's premises in LedearaVere,et have not been re-eccupied till ly!thin the last few days.

VACCINATION: THE RECENT DIVISION IN PARLIAMENT.

Sir.—Considerable t-ni-s-a-p-p-ieher-Qon. exists respecting the significance of the division in the House of Commons on Tuesday, June 19th. Mr. Taylor moved—" That in the opinion of this House, it is inexpedient and unjust to enforce vaccination under penalties upon those who regard it as un- advisable or dangerous." Sir Lyon Playfair moved the following amendment :—" That in the opinion of this House the practice of vaccination has greatly lessened the mortal- ity from smallpox; and the laws relating to it, with such modification as experience may suggest, are necessary for the prevention and mitigation of this fatal and multilative disease." According to the Times' report, Sir C. Dilke said he should support Sir L. Playfair's amendment, which ex- pressed an opinion favourable to the practice of vaccination, with such modification as experience may suggest. Sir Charles believed one of those modifications would be the abolition of repeated penalties, and believing that, he should vote for it. The division then took place. not on Mr. Tay- lor's proposal, but on the amendment, 286 voting for Sir L. Playfair's proposition to 16 against. The House, therefore, distinctly voted in the sense in which Sir C. Dilke under- stood the amendment, namely, that of relieving the people from repeated penalties, which the Government are now pledged to abolish.—Yours truly, ALEX. FORSTER. 19, Regent-st., Earlestown, July 3rd, 1883.

FRODSHXII.

SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The annual SeLMO3S at the Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, were preached on Sunday by the Rev. J. Townend, of Rochdale. J'he ser- vic-s were well attended, and the collections aracunted to £lO 10s. At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, on Monday, John Cor- kin (46), a labourer, pleaded guilty to the charge of having stolen a tab, the property of Henry Edward Haywood, at Frodsfiam, and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. SUDDEN DEATH AT ASTON, NEAR FRODSHAM. Mr. Thomas Corker, an old resident of Frodsham, died very sud- denly, on Tuesday morning, at the house of Mr. John Davies, farmer, Aston. The deceased and his brother had been working for some days at Aston, and on the morning in question they walked from Frodsham to Aston, the de- ceased being a little later than his brother, and on his arrival he made a hearty breakfast and commenced to pre- pare a carpet for laying down, but shortly afterwards com- plained of being unwell, and dropped down and expired, the supposed caul* of death being heart disease. The coroner has been communicated with, but an inquest was , considered unnecessary. PROPERTY SALE.—An important sale of valuable freehold and copyhold farm, dwelling-houses, shops, and land, was held at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsham, on Monday, by Mr. Peter Harrel). The property is situate at Frodsham, Helsby, Manley, Mouldsworth, and Halton, and was offered by the executors of the late Mr. John Wright, of Halton. The following prices were obtained :—Lot 1, a freehold dwelling-house and saddler's shop, in Bridge-lane, Frod- sham. containing 33 perches of land, producing a rental of £l5 per annum, was sold at £325; lot 2, a freehold dwel- ling-house and garden, containing 1 rood 6 perches, situate at the higher end of Main-street, Frodsham, rent £l9, realised £420; lot 3, a freehold cottage adjoining, was sold for £l5; lot 4, a residence at the lower end of Frodsham, containing 1,408 square yards, rent £25, changed hands for £400; lot 5, a piece of freehold meadow land, called the " horse pasture," containing Ba. 2r. 26p., situate in Frodshara Marsh, rent £2O, fetched £520; lots 6 and 7 were put up together, and.consisted of two freehold fields, containing 4a. 2r. 38p., called" Upper and Lower Snidlev Moor," rent £lO, was knocked down for £460: lot 8, the half-part of two meadows at Horn's Mill, Helsbv, containing 12a 2r. 26p., was purchased for £400; lot 9, a small freehold farm and house at Manley, containing Ba. Sr. 30p., rent £3O, realised £875; lot 10, a freehold cottage, with garden, realised £190; lot 11, two freehold cottages, with gardens, containing 2a. Or. 37p., was sold for £310; lot 12 consisted of a free- hold dwelling-house and shop, situate in Halton, and was knocked dawn at £250; lot 13 sold for £105; and lot 14, a freehold residence called" Croten House," with land, stable, and coach-house, containing about four statute acres, was withdrawn at £7OO. The above is the most successful pro- perty sale which has taken place at Frodsham for some time, and there was a large attendance. HOUGHTON GREEN.

PERMITTING D—R-ITN-K-E—NNE- S-S ON LICENSED PREMISES.— Mary Darbyshire, landlady of the Plough Inn, Houghton Green, was, on Wednesday, summoned te the Warrington County Petty Sessions, charged with having allowed drunkenness on her licensed premises. Mr. Robert Davies appeared for the defence.—P.S. Patinson stated that about half-past one o'clock on Sunday, the 17th ult., he passed the Plough Inn, and saw through the window a man named John Validay. About 25 minutes to three on the same afternoon he saw Validay in front of the Plough Inn very drunk, and he had since been fined 5s and costs for the offence. In consequence of information he received he went to the Plough Inn about eight o'clock the same even- ing, and found Validay there very drunk. He called the landlady's attention to the fact, but he was told that Vali- day was not drunk, and he was treated with deGance.—John Validay said he was in the Plough Inn about half-past one, but he was neither drunk nor sober. He was there again in the evening, but he only had twb glasses of beer, and he did not consider he was drunk.—A son of ,defendant's said Validay, along with about eight others, was at the inn at noon, and they were served with three quarts of ale. Vali- day was again there in the evening, but he had only been served with two glasses of ale when the officer entered. He did not consider the man was drunk.—The Bench said they were bound to say that the case was proved, and defendant would be fined 40s and costs, but the license would not be endorsed in consideration of the previous good character of the house.
