The Salvation Army and its doings is the great and moving force here, doing all the excitement in anticipation or otherwise. The " General " Booth was to come on Fri- day. That was sufficient for all kinds of preparations at home and barracks, at shop, in street. Such canvassing— Will you come ?" •' Shall you be there ?" "What a har- vest of " ? To see the man whose fiat is the peace and 'enjoyment of so many !" Well, though prepared for "blood and fire," and any other execution that could be thought of, the army was doomed to disappointment. No General turned up, instead thereof a telegram and Major Taylor., The band, walk, ride, sing, exciting small speeches, boast, and promise, forming such a pabulum that may keep up the excitement without feeding the hunqry souls. Yet they wait till Tuesday, for the verified promise will be, as it proved to many, extension of enjoyment by the prolonga- tion of hope, not deferred too far to make the heart sick. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. ISMATL PASHA AT CREWE WORTS.— Ismail Pasha, ex- Khedive of Kgypt ; Bernhard, Hereditary Prince of Saxe- Meiningen ; Mince Ibrahim Hiliny, Count H. Eismark (son of Prince Bismark), Sefer Pasha and snite, with Colonel Stanley Clarke and General Sir Arnold Burrows Kemball, K.C.8., arrived at Ccewe on Wednesday, and were con- ducted through the steel works by the Duke of Sut!Arland and Mr. F. W. Webb (chief engineer of the London and North-Western Railway). The visitors spent four hours in inspecting the numerous objects et interest ;led watching the process of the manufacture of Bessemer steel, and, after lunching at Mr. Webb's, they took train at three o'clock, and proceeded over the North Stafford Railicay to Trent- ham, the residence of the Duke of Sutherland, whose guests

inspection. The Corporation had no right whatever to have anything to do with the traders unless the traders took in all Warrington for the present and for the future, too. They were gentlemen able to protect them- selves, and why should the Council mix up their contract about sewerage and the like with gentlemen whose only ob- ject was to get a plentiful supply of water and leave none for the others? If they agreed to that they would put a premium upon the works at present existing in Warrington. They would either give them a monopoly which would pre- sent ethers traders coming because they would be unable to work on the same terms, or they entirely forbade them to ' come—and he was sorry to say-he had heard that that was the spirit of some of the traders. The members of the Town Council ought to take a broader and wider view and provide that the river shall never lose one gallon of its water so far as the general consumption by the townspeople was con- cerned. Anything short of that would be wrong, and if they were bound to sign the contract that night they might as well at once put iron collars on their necks, go before the Manchester Canal Company, blow down and worship them as their lords and masters. They had done all t!..ey could be expected to do on behalf of the company, and they were left entirely helpless as far as the explanation of the mayor was concerned. If there was any way out of the difficulty he woultl gladly rejoice, for as it appeared at present it would be a shame—nay, a disgrace—if theysigned their name to any paper that would tie them for all time to a mere supply of one million gallons of water. The mere they looked at the matter the more objectionable it seemed, and he strongly protested against it being signed that night. (Hear. hear.)

they are. OPENING OP CREWE ABATTOI El s —The Crewe Cattle Market Abattoiri were opened on Stturday. Exclusive of a railway siding, the cost of which is borne by the London and North-Western Railway Company, the market has cost £14,000. and is the property of a company. It covers five acres of ground, and is cap ible of extension. There is ac- commodation for 1,500 cattle, 6 000 sheep. 500 calves, and 500 pigs. The market is intended to assist in developing the Irish cattle trade throu.Th the London and North-Wes- tern Railway Company's system, and to open out a trade with Scotland, Wales, and the Midland counties; and the ahtttoirs are to compete for the supplyof dead meat to large towns. Taking into account the vast population of which Crewe is the centre, it is confidently believed that the trade of the market will attain to very large dimensions. ' WIGAN ATIILEtIC FESTIVAL —The eiebth annua! athletic festiy,l, held in connection with the Wigan Cricket Club, has been fixed for S Attain July 28th, and the committee

The MAYOR 8.114 before any one else spoke he should like to be allowed to reply to Councillor Dr. Mackie. Councillor Dr. Mackie bad given vent to what he might almost call indignation at the idea of a body of traders monopolising the water of the river. Councillor Dr. Mackie was labour- ing under a great mistake. The traders had not obtained any such monopoly. The rights to the use of the water were not confined to the gentlemen who were named as the traders of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Those rights were spread all over the town--(hear, hear) ; and everybody in Warrington to-day had as much right tolise that water as any one of the firms named. The traders bad not reserved the rights to themselves or anything of the kind. All that they could obtain was the arrangement stated for the supply of 7 million gallons of water. He might tell the Council that, as far as he was individually concerned, he bad said from the very first that he did not want this pro- posed canal to be made. (Hear, hoar.) He said to the pro- meters " Leave us as we are. We are perfectly content and we don't want to have your canal. We have got good
are sparink no puns to make the meeting a successful one. 'The usual list of valuable pi izs is offered; and nothing but fine weather will be required to maka a satisfactory gathering.

water, and we are certlin of it, but we don't know that we shall be if you make this canal." (Hear, hear.) The Cor- poration thirst nat suppose that the traders of Warrington had been so desperately anxious to have the

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 7 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 7 1883.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. His Worship the Mayor (Councillor Cros- field) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Webster, and Kean; Councillors Monks, Greening, Brown, Sutton, Wright, Bolton, Wm. Pierpoint, Marsh, Wooltall, Mackie, Whittle, Francomb, Burgess, Dixon, Barker, Caldwell, Taylor, and Hutchinson; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), T. Longdin (borough sur- veyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager). THE RECENT ELECTION.
The DEPIIFY Toivx CLERK: I have to report to the Council that Robert William Marsh has been duly elected a councillor for the South-East Ward of this borough. THE SOUTHPORT FORESHORE QUESTION.

The MAYOR said he had received a letter from the Mayor of Southport on the Southport foreshore question. Enclosed was a statement of facts relating to the matter, which had already engaged the attention of Parliament. He (the Mayor of Southport) would feel obliged if the same was read at the meeting of the Council, and a resolutioniaimilar to the one passed by the Manchester City Council was pa ,sed. Cannelnor SorroN asked if there would be any expense at (aiding the support of the matter as requested by the M vor of Southport. The MAYOR replied that it would be no expense to the Council. They would be aware that there had been very considerable feeling expressed in the House of Commons on the matter, and he fancied that they, as a corporation, would sympathise with the Southport Corporation in their efforts to protect their rights connected with the foreshore. (Hear, hear.) Alderman WEBSTER asked if, they had power to pass or support any memorial without suspending the standing orders. The DEPUTY Towx CLERK: Oh, yes. The MAYOR: I will move this resolution, which is similar to the one passed by the Manchester Council :—" That a memorial under the corporate seal be presented to the Prime Minister respectfully asking the exercise of his influence to prevent the foreshore at Southport being alienated by Her Majesty's Government, and passing entirely into private control, and urging that the foreshore in question is of enor- mous importance to millions of persons, and especially to the industrial population ot Lancashire; and that it should be entrusted to the Corporation of Southport for the purpose of being dealt with by that body, from time to time, under the sanction and authority of Parliament, in such a manner I as may be deemed necessary in the interests of the public." Alderman WEnsTER seconded the motion, and said he ; thought the Chancellor of the Duchy had made a great mistake in actin.- in (ho manner he had done. It had placed the Southport Corporation in a very unpleasant' position, and he thought the Corporation of Warrington should sup- port them to the utmost of their power in their endeavours to obtain possession of the foreshore. He would like to add that the representative of Warrington in Parliament be re- quested to support the memorial in every possible way. The MAYOR : Yes. We shall send it to the member for the time being to present. Alderman WEBSTER :If he be requested to support it, it will be better, Ithink. The MAYOR: We will see that it is done. The motion was then carried. THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME AND THE RIVER. LIVELY DISCUSSION.

canal made, and to make this stipulation for the supply of 7 million gallons of water. Nothing of the kind. If they were put to the expense of maintain- ing their rights, and of claiming this minimum quantity of seven million gallons of water, was it fair that some manu- facturer should come in the future and take out of this supply of water such a quantity as would cripple the old firms in their supply? That was the view that the members had to take of the matter. As for selling the rights of the Corporation of Warrington, they were not doing anything of the sort. The Corporation of Warrington had not any right whatever over the water in the river. The rights in the water of the river were riparian rights; they did not be- long to the Corporation. As for talking of the traders as if they were a band of selfish men, who were just thinking of their own interests and no one else's, why, it was ridiculous to talk in that manner. Every person in Warrington who had any riparian right to the water would have that right hereafter. They could not do more than that. The signing of the agreement on the part of the Corporation was a mere matter of form. It re- ferred more particularly to the Corporation sewers and roads than to their right to the use of water. This water question was more especially a trader's question. (Hear, hear.) The Corporation really had no power whatever re- specting it. The Corporation had, he could tell them, done their very best to claim everything that they thought they had a right to claim; and he could only tell them what the town clerk had told him, that in the committee-room of the House of Commons the town clerk was congratulated on the splendid terms that the Warrington people had got, for it was considered Warrington was a great deal better treated than any other town. He would be very sorry to be a party to anything which would sacrifice any right that the people of Warrington enjoyed. He would be one of the very last to do such a thing. There was nobody valued the privileg's of the - river more than he did. He knew the value of them, and he knew the value they would be to future generations. As to saying that he was going to shut out other manufacturers for the town, did they think that he was afraid of some other soap-maker coming to establish works in Warrington? Soap-makers might come as SOOR as they liked, but if they came and could not get water where his firm's works were, they must go higher up the river. Then as to the supposition that they conld not get seven million gallons of water, he might tell the Council seven million gallons was three or four times the quantity of water the works at present used ; and there was no likelihood of the existing works being en- larged to such an extent that they would consume the whole of that quantity of water. It might be 20 , or it might be 500 years before the water was required. Councillor Mame:: I understood your first answer to me was, that the water was confined to the gentlemen named.

The MAYOR: No, no. Councillor MACKIE said it would satisfy all of them, and the town generally, if they knew that the seven million gallons were at the direction of the Town Council, to be distributed as they thought fit; or, at least, that they had a hand in it. The MAYOR could not tell Councillor Dr. Mackie that. He did not see that the Corporation would have any-control over the seven million gallons at all any more than they had at present over the water in the river. They had now none at all.

Councillor Bunoxss thought everyone on the banks of the river had riparian rights to the water of the river. In fact, no one else had any right to it; but at the same time, there were manufacturers in the town who got water, and they had no riparian rights. If they took the water through the town they could only take it by the sancti6n of the Corporation. The MAYOR: Hear, hear. That is quite true. Councillor BURGESS thought that if the ship canal was made it would take away the present banks of the river as far as Warrington was concerned, and would, therefore, de— stroy the riparian rights that already existed. The irIAYOR : The river will be along Arpley fields. Alderman HOLMES pointed out-that it was only in case of the water in the river failing that the 7 million gallons weuld be wanted. If the river remained as it was at pre- sent there would he no use of the other supply. _ . . _ _

The MAYOR said all .riparian rights aC Present existing would be maintained, and the whole of the shore, if it was made into a canal, along Arpley up to the weir would be reserved—that was to say, the Manchester Ship Canal Co. could not claim the banks as a wharf.

Councillor BURGESS thought if the ship canal was made and there was to be such a failure in that part of the river, it would be impossible for anyone excepting those people having rights on the banks of the river to get the water. He did not sec why it should not be secured to the whole of the town.

Councillor SUTTON said the same point had occurred to him. Although it had been said that they were not to in- terfere with the riparian rights of owners of property on the banks of the Mersey, still it must be admitted that some- body had considered it was necessary to enter into the agreement, and the Corporation, being a party to it, must have some interest in it. Of course they all thought the Corporation was professing to look after the interests of the whole of the borough. It was quite clear from the agree- ment that whatevez benefit there was was to be confined to the manufacturerslnd traders DOW carrying on business, and that In one else could really be permitted to par- ticipate in the benefits. The MAYon : But there are riparian rights secured. Councilivr If the riparian rights are to be in one case, why ark, they not in every case. If you mairaain that there is no nec..e3ity for this agreement, why bring it in at all? Someone must consider that they are being benefited by this agreement. The MAYOR: Excuse me interrupting you. If it bad not been that see as traders formed a cotna.ittee among our- selves, and went to the expense we have done, you would have had no stipulation as regards the water in the river at all.

Councillor MACKIE: I bag your pardon. 'f he Mayor:: The Corporation could not have dona P. ; Councillor SUTTON said that the interest of everybody in ; Warrington should be considered in the matter of this ship ! canal, and in anything pertaining to it. But this agreement clearly reserves the water to the present traders, and keeps out everybody else who have at present rights. But what would they be hereafter when the ship canal is made ? What rights would the owners of property have if the agreement with the ship canal were made? They could not be in the same position as they were now.
The MAYOR You don't seam to understand that these gentlemen whose names are down here are merely acting as trustees for the rest of the manufacturers of the town.

Councillor SUTTON asked why did it not sty so? H they had added to the present traders," also their successors and assigns, "and all persons who might have an interest in pro- perty, then the whole thing would have been right. If the clause had been a little plainer the whole thing would have been correct, and there would have been no questiomabout it. Coancipor Bovrox protested against any committee acting for the whdle boron:A, especially when they began to barter rights and privileges which belonged to the rate- payers of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR: I am sorry you were not on that committee.

Councillor Bburox said he sent a letto rto Mr. Jos. Davies on April 4th. in which he drew attention to a privilege they at present enjoyed. It wasin reference to srnallboats and other craft, the owners of which could enjoy the use of the river up to the weir without tell. The consmfftee, however, had simply entered into a contract for ever that all small boats or craft going down without goods should pay 5s every time they usPd the locks at Walton. He enjoyed a stil down the river, but would not like to pay 103 for what he had hitherto enjoyed for nothing. He considered, the com- mittee had gone 6Pyond their duties, especially when they hiel the suggestion he had made in their minds. He thought the Corporation ought not to be told that the thing was cut and dried, and that they had no voice in the matter.

Councillor MONKS said it was unfortunate that the Town Clerk, or the person responsible for the agreement being in the form it was, did not see that the Corporation and the traders' question were not mixed up together. (Applause.) However, he protested against the assumption that the traders bad been bartering the interests of Warrington at large for their own selfishipurpoaes. He could assure them that there was no such an idea, but they had doae what any man sitting round that table would do and that was, protect their own interests as far as they possibly could, and it was for that Council to protect their interests as far as the matter affected the Corporation. The question of the quantity of water was one which he pressed very strongly at the meeting with the caaal company, because there were times, even now, when they had a very high tide, when the water was to some extent affected by the salt. , He thought they were, therefore, only acting as sensible and prudent men in requiring that in the event of a larger quantity of salt water coming up the river than usual they should be protected against having to use it. It was a provision that if the water was so affected, as he believed it would be, then the manufacturers now using the water should have a prior claim to the wafer sent from above for their own purposes. He did not exictly agree with the Mayor's interpretation of the clause, for he did not fe.l called upon to subscribe money now for the benefit of every man who might choose to come to Warrington hereafter. The MAYOR: I said that we have stipulated for the rights of everybody now at work in Warrington, but not for any- body who chooses to set up works hereafter. Councillor Momrs maintained that if he subscribed any money now. in connection with that matter it was because they would have a prior claim over any new comer. It was all very well to come there and talk about the future manu- facturers of Warrington, but he thought they had more to fear from the grasping, avaricious owners of the land than anybody else. He t,oought-there was some misapprehension with reference to the seven million gallons. He believed they would have not only enough, but a great deal more than they would require. If they were to develop° the manufacturers of Warrington they must feel secure that they would receive a qnantity of water as good as that they now received—and plenty of it. They were only acting as men of prudence and common-sense in seeking to protect their interest, and he did not thillk they ought to be con- demned as avaricious traders seeking to grasp everything for themselves. After all, it was a question of everybody look- ing after their own interests. Councillor BCRGESS : I should like to know if any per- sons in the future wbo may have riparian rights on the banks of the river will be entitled to any portion of these seven million gallons? I think not. The MaYort: That is rather a conundrum, Councillor Burgess. (Laughter.) Councillor BGROES : I will put it a little plainer. Will they have the same right to any portion of the seven mil- lion gallons?

The MAYOR: Yes they would. Councillor BURGESS: Do you mean to tell me that her people will have the right? The MAYOR: Yes, that is how I understand it. Councillor BURGESS: lam quite certain that this agree- ment will not give them the right. Councillor BARKER maintained that if anyone had rights on the banks of the river they had rights to the water. Comacillor BURGESS said the agreement only applied to the traders and inanufacturers.

The DEPUrY TOWN CLERB;tid as far as he understood it, and he thought the Town Clerk was of the same opinion, the seven million gallons were secured to the present manu- facturers using the water from the river, and those who pos- sessed riparian rights. Councillor BURGESS: Those who possess them in the future?

The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK : Yes. This agreement has been prepared by counsel in the ordinary way, and the Town Clerk, for anything in it, is not responsible. Councillor SurroN : Is there any probability of getting words inserted which will give the privilege to the persons who have riparian rights, in addition to the persons men- tioned in the agreement? The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: It is now out of your power to do that.

Councillor CALDWELL asked if Warrington was going to be restricted to seven million gallons of water for the present traders, and if others were not to get any benefit? If that was so he thought it would be better to say that in future. the population of Warrington instead of increasing would decrease. It seemed a strange thing that, a place like Warrington, second to none for its size and the multiplicity of its industries, was to be bound to seven million gallons of water for the present manufacturers.
The MAYOR: You are labouring under a delusion. You say to be limited to seven million gallons. It is not to be limited to _seven million gallons.
Councillor MACKIE :It says "not exceeding seven mil— lions."

The MAYOY : Excuse me. These seven million gallons have to be brought from above the weir, and it is to be of the mine quality as the water is now. In addition to these seven million gallons there will be hundreds of millions of gallons of. water.

Councillor CALDWELL thought that simplified the whole thing. Supposing that in the future other manufacturers came, would they have the right or privilege of getting the water at their own expense? The MAYOR: Of ccurse they have. I must remind the Council of this, that this agreement has, and all these clauses have been gone over, over and over again, by men of great commercial experience, aided by legal knowledge, and that every stipulation and every protection that could be thought of has been put into it. (hear, hear.) If you think by reading it over you can improve it and make it better it is a great mistake. In these matters we are bound to trust in a great measgre to legal advisers. It has not been done in haste—there has been a great amount of time spent over it. You may speak for a month, and probably you will not make it any better. Councillor SUTTON: As the agreement cannot be altered, I think we are bound to accept it. Councillor BURGESS: I shall vote against it. The MAYOR did not personally care a penny-piece whether it was sanctioned or not.

Alderman WEBSTER said the agreement spoke of the traders and manufacturers generally. It never could be intended, and was never the intention of the committee that the seven million gallons should be simply confined to persons now resident in the borough. if that were so it would be a ridiculous agreement to make. The Corporation was supporting the traders for the purpose of continuing the riparian rights not enly for the parties living at the present day, but others to come after them. It could not be said that they were banded together to prevent others in the future. If anyone came and obtained riparian rights; and had a manufactory on the river—whether iron, soap. india- rubber, or anything elsa—they would have, or ought to have, an equal right to the water for their boilers with those who were now contending for the right and protection of it from the canal company. If they had not, Warrington would simply be confined to its present number of manu- factories, and anyone could see in a moment that Warring- ton never could increase under those circumstances in the way it should do. The MAYOR: You are overlooking the fact that the river will remain there still. These seven million gallons may never, and probably never will be wanted. Alderman WEBSTER : I should say that this Corporation cannot sanction any agreement that does not secure a right to this seven million gallons to every manufacturer who has, or who in the future will have, riparian rights. Councillor GREENING asked them to suppose for moment that the present manufacturers had used up all the water and another manufacturer came to the town, built a manu- factory on the river, and obtained riparian rights. Ire would like to know if the new manufacturers would have any participation in the seven million gallons. Where would he get his water from ? The MAYOR: Ile must build his works according to the water.

Councillor GREENING said it had been stated that if the present manufacturers used all the water, the other people would find plenty of water in the river. But he guessed it would be of such a quality that they would not be able to use it, so that he slid not see that the future generations would benefit anything if they did obtain riparian rights. If the seven million gallons was not for the henetit•of the whole of the town iC was not right. At the present moment the Warrington Waterworks Company were opposing the clause in question, and he thought their opposition was grounded on the seven million gallons. The Corporation had instructed counsel to support the clause, and who was eci bear that expense ? He thought it was to come out of the rates. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: The Town- Clerk has ai- r° idy instructed counsel to appear on behalf of the Corpora- tion, as well as on behalf of the manufacturers. They will support the arrangements made with the Promoters with respect to the seven million gallons, and matters generally. It is quite true, as the Mayor said, that the Corporation had no locus stradi to appear before the committee of the House of Commons upon the seven million gallons of water, or respecting the rights of the river at. all. It is in the wiedom of the Council embodied in the agreement. I think it is a' little ;beyond the province of the Council to discuss the question of the supply of seven million gallons. It is a question which the manufacturers themselves have brought forward and secured, not only to themselves, but to the riparian owners on the river. Councillor GREENING said they were representatives of the whole town and they came there to further the interests of the town. He thought a way to do so was to protect the rights and privileges they had at present. The M.t.vort: As a Corporation we have no locus standi before the Committee of the House of Commons as regards this water question. The traders have had to look after their own interests independent of the Corporation, and if the traders of 'Warrington had not banded themselves to- gether to protect their own interests you might then have crud out at,out what the future of Warrington would have been.

Councillor MACKIE said it was very desirable that the Council should come to a decisive and friendly vote that night, and he therefore moved as an amendment that such parts of the agreement as did not refer to the seven million gallons of water be only approved. The Mayon: I must repeat what you mast see for your- selves, that before the Committee of the House of Commons the Corporation would not have a locus standi as regards this water question. Councillor Macau: Excuse me. You are quite wrong there lam sure you are. Councillor BURGESS : Do you mean to tell me if we go to protect the right of Warrington in the river that the Com- mittee will tell us lye have no right to appear there to protect it? The MAYOR: Yes. Several members here rose to speak, but the Mayor asked for "one at a time, please," and called upon Councillor Breower, who took it that the instruction give to the Town Clerk was to protect the whole of the borough of Warrington in reference to the supply of water suitable for manufacturers. lie had a clear recollection that that was the Town Clerk's instruction, and he gathered in attending the meetings tied the opposition to their obtaining a supply of suitable water for the manufacturers came from the Warrington Waterworks Company, and not from the Ship Canal Company. The Ship Canal Cornpany, so far as he had been able to gather, had been quite willing to treat the manufacturers of the borough and the Corporation with very great fairness. Councillor Morms still held to the opinion that the agree- rnent was intended for the benefit of the present traders. The MAYOR could only tell the members for their conso- lation that the possibility of the seven million gallons of water being required was almost as remote as one of the planets. lie might tell them for their further consolation it was only in case the water in the river was brackish and not fit for steam boiler purposes that the Ship Canal Company. undertake to bring down a culvert water from above the weir that would be of suitable quality to supply the manu- facturers of Warrington. But they should remember that the river would still remain; it was not going to be done away with. They should also remember that the first time the -Counail met the promoters in that Council Chamber he said to Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, "there is one thing that we must have above -everything else, and that is, we must have as geod o; supply Of the same qeality of water from the river as we lleve now for steam boiler purposes." (Hear, hear.) That was the first stipula- tion he made when he met Mr. Leader Williams, and the Connell might trust to the manufectuters and legal gentle- men together having made the very beet arrangement that was possible under the circumstances. If the members of the Council thought they could draw up a better agreement with the promoters of the ship canal than that set forth they were quite at liberty to do so—only they were too late ! (Laughter.) Councillor MACKIR : We are not at liberty, Mr. Mayor, if we were we could do it. Councillor Witerrex : You have spoken once or twice. I object to this entirely, for I want to make a speech. (Laughter.) _

„. Councillor MACKIE said he would listPn to Councillor Whittle, or anyone else, but be prayed they veould remember they bad the interests of Warrington at stake. Councillor WHITTLE: We have rules. Councillor MACKIE : Nover mind rules in o case like ibis.

The DEPUTY Tows elms, replying to Councillor -clacitie, said the resolution was simply to place the common seal to the agreement. They could add no rider to that.. The agreement, of course, bound the Corporation so far as was expressed in the agreemnt itctlf, and no further,

Councillor &MGM did not agree to the signing of the agreement, because he did not think the clauses right. The DEPUTY Towx CLERK said they had been approved by the General Purposes Committee. The MAYOR: It is a strange thing to me that there is more wisdom in this Council Chamber than outside it. It is a remarkable thing that though the traders themselves and the ablest counsel that we could find in London, having put their heads together, have framed these clauses and made these stipulations, yet there are gentlemen in this Council Chamber who say they could have done a great deal better. (Hear. hear.) I think the Council is to be con- gratulated that we have got men of such great ability. Councillor BARKER: Councillor Dixon has been on his legs a quarter of an hour. Let him speak. Alderman KEAN : He is a very patient man. Councillor DIXON, referring to the water obtained from the river, said there were names of firms on the list that he remembered formerly did not get a bucketful of water from the river.
• The MAYOR: That has nothing to do with the question at all.
Councillor SurroN asked whether thy were bound to vote for the agreement as a whole, or whether they could take out any part of it, and what would be the effect if they did not agree to it ?

The MAYOR s,iid, as far as he understool the matter, if the Council did not sanction the signing of the agreement his common sense would tell him that the whole thing was at an end—(hear, hear)—and that the Manchester Ship Canal promoters could go and do as they liked. Councillor Surrox Well, that will influence me in my vote.

The Meson said that was as he underitood the matter. He could tell the Council his sympathies were entirely with the inhabitants of Warrington—(hear, hear)—as to preserv- ing the rights to the use of the river, and if they had any respect for his opinion on the subject—he had a great deal of bother about it in one way or another—they might rest content that the privileges they at present enjoyed would not be interfered with if the canal was made. He felt pretty confident of that; if he did not feel so he would move heaven and earth to stop it. (Hear, hear.) He believed they would be all right, and he thought the members might make their minds quite easy on the subject. Councillor FRA.NCOMB asked WAS It not possible to ad- journ the discussion. _ _

- The Mayon: No, it must be concluded to—night. Councillor FRANCOMB had always understood that the ship canal would bring to Warrington a number of other manufacturers, and if the water was spoiled for manufac- turing purposos.then for the future they would be limited to a supply of 7 million gallows. (Cries of " Yes" and " No.") The Mayor and Councillor Monks were certainly against each other on that point, but if they were limited in the future to a supply of 7 million gallons he thought it would be a fatal day for Warrington if they signed that agree- ment.

I;OURCiIiOr BURGESS then rose, and was met with the re- mar : "von can't speak again !" 'He, however, said the Ma ~r had spoken several times, and as he put things in a di c3rent light, he thought he ought to be able to speak. The Mayor told them unless they agreed to the agreement that night the Ship Canal Company would do what they liked. He begged to tell the Council that if they did not wiree to the resolution it was not at all likely that the House of Comtnens would agree to the Ship Canal Bill un- til some agreement had been come to with them. There- fore, he did not think the division ought to be taken with- out that fact being taken into consideration. The MAYOR said when gentlemen asked him questions it was his bounden duty to answer them. When he was asked a straightforward question he gave a straightforward answer, and he said if they did not sign the agreement common sense would tell anyone that the matter must be at an end. ("No, no.") They should remember that the clauses of the agreement had been gone into by the General Purposes Committee, and that committee was considered to have the authority of the Council to do its business. (No, no.") Well, then, the General Purposes Committee had better not exist.
The DEPUTY Tows CLERK pointed out that in tbe agreement were embodied terms that had been discussed time after time in the Council Chamber and in committee.

Councillor Burgess said if the General Purposes-Commit- tee could do without the consent of the Council they had no right to pass the resolution. The DEPUTY Towx CLERK: That is so. Councillor BURGESS: Then why do you want the sanction of the Council to confirm it?
The MAYOR: It is simply formal piece of business. (Loud cries of "divide.") After a few words from Alderman Webster, . _ _
The MAYOR Enid te thought they had discusscd the matter long enough, and he should put the resolution to the meeting.... . _

Councillor MicKIE objected to this matter being hurried on, and he objected strongly against several gentlemen calling out "divide." [Councillor WHITTLE: Another speech.] This was a matter of which the success of War- rington was at stake, and in spite of what Councillor Whittle might interpose he maintained that it ought to he argued to the last. Their only safety was in an adjourn- ment.

The MAYOR said he had let three or four gentlemen speak twice, because he was very anxious to make the mind of the members easy on the subject. Councillor itioNKs said if they were to suspend the stand- ing orders they would 13.,3 in order, and they could stay all night if they _wanted.

bauncillor Ilarrcumsox said in his opinion the period when they would require the seven million gallons of water was very remote, and he thought that if ever they.requir,,d a greater quantity thiy would be able to get it. But he could not get over the riparian rights of the river. If he could be assured that future manufacturers building works on the river would have equal rights to the seven million gallons of water wi:h the present manufacturers he should certainly vote in favour of the resolution.

Councillor Surrog said as nothing else could be done, he would have to vote in favour of the resolution. Councillor BARKER: You had better have seven million gallons than none at all. Councillor BURGESS: I want them all to nave it. Why should one have it and not another?

Councillor WRIGHT asked was it not possible at this st.ige for the agreement to be amended, so that the whole of the manufacturers of the town could participate in the supply of rater. Councillor MONKS: Will all the manufacturers subscribe to the cost?

Councillor WRlGiri: did not see why he should not have the same right as other manufacturers to the use of thewater in the river; and he asked was it not in the power of the Council to protect other manufacturers besides those who were now interestod in the river?

The MAYOR said he bad explained half a dozen 'times that night, as well as he could, that the Corporation had no locus standi as regards the water of the river, and the rights as to the use of that water had to be protected by the traders. Of course' the Council assisted as far as they could, but they could not go into the connnittee-room at the House of Commons—at least, that was as he under- stood it—because they had no locus standi. Councillor WRIGHT remarked that there seemed to be selfishness on the part of the present traders that they could not obtain for other manufacturers the same rights that they had secured to themselves.

Councillor BURGESS asked, if the Council had no locus standi, how could they be parties to an agreement? The MAYOR: Excuse me, Councillor Burgess, I have to!d you before to-night that when I speak of having a locus standi I mean in the committee-room of the House of Com- mons. There is nothing to prevent an argument being carried on or an agreement being entered into outside that committee-room between the Council of the Corporation and the promoters of the ship canal; but it is a very different thing when you get into the committee-room of the House of Commons. With my humble ability I have done all I can, and I do not see if we sit here all night that we shall get any nearer. Councillor MACKIE aslced for the clause to be read which prevented an adjournment. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK replied that there was no clause which prevented the discussion being adjourned, hut the resolution should be passed at once as the bill would he before the House of Commons on the following day. After a little further discussion

Councillor BURGESS warmly objected to the Deputy Town Clerk asking him net to mislead the Council. He was not doing anything of the sort. He said they were asked to agree to certain clauses which were binding on the Corporation clearly, and he objected to be told by the Dunn ty Town Clerk or anyone else that he was trying to mislead the Corporation when he was pointing out those clauses which were objectionable. The MAYOR: I can only say, gentlemen, it you don't agree to this agreement to. night you will make a great mis- take. That is my opinion. I shall now put it to the Council, and you can vote upon it. A MEMBER: I should like to ask a question. The MAYOR: I shall not answer another quez-tion. I have said quite enough.

The vote wae-thea taken. Councillor MAcKnt said, his vote must not be taken as in any way finding fault with the promoters cf the Manchester Ship Canal. If they had had the question adjourned, which it seemed could ho done, they should have been prepared to have maintained their position. Councillor CAL/ME:I said, as the navor had allowed Di. Mackie to give an explanation—(interruption)—be wishcd to state he gave his on the dietiuct understanding from the Mayor that the future manufacturers would have the right to tap the water on the:: own account up river.

The MAYOR anaounCed that I 6 members had voted, for, and six against, the resolution, which he declared carried. For: The Mayer, Aldermen Holmes, Webster, and Kean; Councillors Sutton, Woolfall, Ta.ylor, Marsh. Hutchinson, Brown, Monica, Whittle, William Pierpoint, Barker, Dixon, and Caldwell-16. Against: Councillors Mackla,, Burgess. Oreening, Wright. Bolton, and Francomb-6. Councillor Monts: Now, Mr. Mayor, will you permit another explanation? (Loud laughter.) Councillor MACKIE : Quite right. It is an important affair.

Councillor MONKS: I and other traders felt our grievance to be this. .We have already subscribed to the promotion of the ship canal, and we have had to subscribe to protect our. own interests. I think it is -

Councillor SUTTON : Will you also remind Counc.llor Monks that to a great extent the expenses have come Out of the Corporation's pocket—(hear, hear) ; and that; both in the Council Chamber and in other ways, the r,:;orporation have assiated In order to obtain those tights? And yet ho grumbiel at having to pay f.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT THE COBDEN

CLUB DINNER. Mr. Chamberlain made an important speech at the annual banquet of the Cobden Club on Saturday. The right hon. gentleman said that nothing had occurred since Mr.Cobden's death to weaken the force of the argument for Free Trade. He (Mr. Chamberlain) frankly owned that he did not regret the slow progress of conviction among other nations, for he looked forward with anxiety and alarm to the time when our merchants and manufacturers would have to face the free competition of Americans. Having alluded to the se- cession of Mr. Goschen and others, and attributed it to the timidity which induced people to fall out of the ranks" at the first suspicion of a forward movement," Mr. Chamber- lain went on to define very clearly the position, the hopes, and the aims of the Radical party in the Cabinet and in Parliament. Party union, he said, was based upon mutual concession,and if the Radicals yielded their liberty of action in the present, they claimed freedom of opinion as to the future. Radicals were always in advance. It was their business to pave the way for future progress. and if that right was denied them union with the less adv'anced members of the party was impossible. It was as insulting to their common sense as injurious to their honour to suppose "that Radicals will be bribed by office to be unfaithful to their cherished principles." Sir Charles Mike described the work which has been done by the Foreign Office in the way of commercial negotiations, and mentioned in connection with the new Anglo-Italian treaty that that instrument, for the first time in the history of such agreements, contains a general arbitration clause under whiCh all future differences between the two countries are to be decided. Sir Charles proposed a toast in honour of America. Mr. T. li. Shearman, one of the American guests, said that the justice and soundness of the doctrines of Free Trade would eventually tell upon his countrymen. He mentioned that in the highly protected cotton manufacturing districts of America wages were 20 per cent. less than those now paid in Lancashire. Lord Houghton, Sir S. Samuel, and Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., also addressed the company. The hon. member for Rochdale said, amid applause, that he should be glad to follow in the wake of the "daring duck- ling."

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS. Mr. Meadowcroft presided over the monthly meeting of the Board, which was held on Wericesdav afternoon. There were also present Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. T. Norman, W. P. Speakman, F. A. Lake, R. Shaw, J. Pritchard, P. itrisca,, J. Williams, W. Brookes (secretary), and M. Barker (surve:-or)

THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. MOM:UTZ, the medical officer, presented his monthly report, which stated that the number of deaths registered in Itar.crn during the past month amounted to 23. One death occurred at Halton-within-Runcorn. Of the above deaths five ware due to chest affections, four to brain diseases, three platsbi2is, two abdoniinal complaints, four marasmus, two senile decay, while scarlatina, whooping cough, and disease of heart accounted for one each, representing a death rate of 18 per 1,000 per annum. Eleven deaths occurred am)ag children five years and under, and eight below one year. Green vegetables and unripe fruit should be avoided during this sultry weather, and all liquid evacutions should bzt se_urated with crude carbolic acid.

- - FEMALE SUFFRAGE Mi Lydia E. Becker wrote to the secretary of the Board nzlst tr; the propriety of adopting a petition to the House of .1, ~on 3 in favour of Mr. Hugh Mason's motion to It • lade in the House of Commons on the t :Jet. asking that the Parliamentary franchise zaLeull beextended to women who possessed the qualification wlitch entitled men to vote, and who had in all matters of local govetnment•had the right to vote.—Dr. 11LteDouGam, naowd that the petition lie on the table. It was, he said, the first time within his memory that any vestion of politics hal been brought before the Board. He did not think that pubic bodies did themselves or their constitutents any great adv.tlitage when they allowed themselves to dabble in Im- perial politics. Politics, in his humble judgment, ought to be exs.lluded not only from municipal councils but also from bodies like their own. Individually they might be of opinion that female suffrage ouglot to be granted, and many of them might be gallant enough to think that some women deserved it, but he was quite sure that others did not any more than diA many members of the male sex.—Mr. BRISCOE seconded the motion, which was carried. SOUTHPORT FORESHORE. A. circular letter was read from the Mayor of Southport, asking the Board to adopt a resolution to be forwarded to the Premier on the foreshore question, but on the motion of Dr. MaaDono.a.LL, who said the Southport Corporation had only themselves to blame for the dilemma they had got themselves into, and condemned the manner in which they -were harassing Her Majesty's Government. THE PUBLIC OFFICES. On the minutes of the last monthly meeting being read, Dr. MacDouGatt said the county authorities had agreed to purchase the Board's offices for the sum which they were offered to them, namely, £5OO. He thought such a con- clusion must be satisfactory to the Board and to the rate- payers.

SCA.RLATINL—THE BRIDGE SLOPE. The Highway and Sanitary Committee's minutes con- tained the following report from the Medical Officer with respect to the recent prevalence of scarlatina, and the sec- retary was ordered to forward a copy to the Local Govern- ment Board :—" From the registrars return of deaths for quarter ended 31st March, 1883. 1. find 17 were attributed to scarlatina in the urban district of Runcorn. No deaths took place in Runcorn during the month of April, and only one during the month of May from scarlatina. The number of non-fatal cases of scarlet fever it is impossible for me to state. Mv four brother practitioners residing in Runcorn keep such cases dark, and in a great many instances the first intimation I receive is in the registrar's return of deaths. When I hear of any outbreak of the above I visit the locality, and give directions to the surveyor to have house sewers and ashpits thoroughly disinfected, and also that the watering cart be well dosed with carbolic acid, and used frequently in th 3 infected streets." The Chairman reported that arrangements had been made for the Bridge Slope to be opened for traffic not later than the 20t1 June. Resolu- tion that a letter be sent to Mr. Victor Clolus requiring him ta abate a nuisance emanating from the Glycerine works.— Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. WILLIAMS seconded the adop- tion of the minutes.—Mr. SHAW congratulated Mr. P. Speakman on the success which had attended his •efforts for the erection of the Bridge Slope. It was of great con- venience for the people of Runcorn, and be believed Mr. Speakman took some interest in the matter in its earlier stages, and he was sure they were much indebted to him for what he had done.—Dr. MAcDouoaLL, while congratula- ting Mr. Speakman, who, he thought, had taken a principal part in this scheme, and to whom they all felt grateful, they ought not to forget the name of Mr. Norman, who had also taken an active part in the matter.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN ob- served that the idea originated with some members of that Board, and it was only when he saw that houses were about to be built on the spot that he actively participated in the scheme. He met the Chairman of the London and North- Weqern Railway at Chester, and put the subject strongly before him, the consequence being that Mr. Moon took away with him a little plan of his (Mr. Speakman's) own, and they now had the slope in its present aspect. He was mach obliged to Mr. Shaw and the members for their cour- teous acknowledgment of his strvicee which were actively atiared in by Mr. Norman after his return from Chester. If it had not ben for M. Farrell, who generously g4ve the land necessary, hP thought it right to say the slope could not have been erectf..d.—The minutes were passed.
THE CANAL BOAIS ACT.

The Cenal Boat COmmittee stated that letters ha 4 been received from the members for Mid-Cheshire, and Mr Burt. with reference to the Canal Boats Act (1878) Amendment Bill, and Mr. P. epeakmen was requested, when in London, giving evidence on the bill to get clause 5 amended or struck out.—Accounts amounting to LW de. 91. on loan account were forwarded for payment. —lt was recom- mended that the law clerk be instructed to pre- pare an agreement to be entered into by Mr. W. Dalziel . as caretaker of the Hospital premises.— Mr. FISHER moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, the adop- tion of the minutes.—Mr. SILS.W thought an agreement un- necessary in regard to the caretaker. In his opinion, agree- ments were too frequently made where a simple resolution would be sufficient for all purposes, and it was so in this in- stance. It was an expense that did not need to be incurred, and he would move that the minute referring to the matter be referred back.—Mr. Faluft recognised the force of Mr. Shaw's objection, but stated it was the general wish of the committee than an agreement sheuld be drawn up, so that they might remove the caretaker at any time they wished. There was sometimes a difficulty in removing people from premises. Ha agreed that the minute should he referred back, which was done.—ln answer to a question from Dr. MacDougall, Mr. PRITCHARD said the Bill with regard to the Canal Boats Act affected Runcorn considerably, the town being, as it were, the depot of a great number of boats. He supposed that between 700 and 800 boats were registered in Runcorn, and if this Bill was passed into law the Govern- ment coul 1 send their inspector at any time they thought proper to hold an inquiry and charge the local authority with the expenses. The committee thought that clause rather hard, and desired it to be struck out, and the expense of the inquiries to be boine by the Imperial Exchequer. Mr. Speakman was going to London, and he promised the committee that be would do what he could in the matter free of expense to the Board.—Dr. MACDOUGALL read clause .5 of the Bill, which, it appeared, provided for strict inquiry • into the sanitary, moral, and educational condition of canal boats and thefr inhabitants, only the 4th section referring to the financial question; and yet, remarked the doctor, the , committee, without explanation, desired the whole clause to be struck out. It seemed to him that those who desired to promote a better state of things on board boats were particu- larly anxious that the Local Government 'Board as well as the Education Department should have a say as to how the Act was carried out by the local authorities, Ile did not wish to reflect upon the way in which the Committee discharged its duties in connection with the administration of this Act, but it was somewhat singular that according to the report of their own inspector, seven offences had ' been committed last month, and not a single prosecution had been undertaken. The speaker pointed out that the Bill provided for the levy- ing of fees upon the boats to meet the charges of the en- quiries. Mr. Speakman, as a boat owner, naturally was going to London to give evidence against the Bill, and was perfectly right in doing that, but bow could he at the same time appear for the Board? It was impossible for him to appear in the dual character. He (the speaker) contended that it was no part of the duty of that Board to take any pertwith the boat-owning authorities in that or any other Own. These people were perfectly capable of taking care of themselves. (Hear, hear.) Re took it that the Board was willing to see-the boat people more humanely treated than they were some time ago, not only as to sanitary arrangements, but morally and educationally, and he moved that the resolution be referred back.—The CHAIRMAN did not think the town would suffer by the course taken by the committee. The resolution was perhaps a little Irregular and oueht to have stated " section four of clause s."—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said as his name had been vaent'oned—[Dr. MacDottuAnn : I did not take exception to you3—he wished to explain that as he was going to London the committee rtqueated him to use his good offices in this matter, and he promised to do so. He stated that if the Bill were i:rpsed as it at present stood, any common infor- mer prowling around the boats and finding some little Irregularity, would get halt the fee, and a Government in- spector would be sent down to hold an inquiry at the cost of Runcorn He took it that at the present moment the b )at class were the bread winners for Ituncorn.—Dr. MAC- DOUGALL : We have registered 500 boats thate Rancorn has no interest in.—Me. SPEAKMAN : But we have to look after them. The Board were opposing the Bill to protect them- selves,—Dr. MACDOUGALL : They ought to take a more efficient step then.—Mr. SPEARMAN then charged the Dr. with inconsistency.-Mr. FISHER explained that the 7 offences to which Dr. MacDougall had referred were of so frivoloas a nature that they were left in the hands of the inspector, who could easily deal with them. The committee wished to work in a friendly manner with the boat owners, same as one gentleman would with another, and not be continually putting them to the expense of appearing before the magis- trates. The committee did not object to the Lecal Govern- ment Board sending down inspectors, but they did not want them to teuch the pockets of the Runcorn ratepayers, and they had as much right to protect the boat-people of Run- corn as they bad to protect themselves against the pro- moters of the ship canal. He objected to an annual charge beiag levied on the boat-owners for the sake of complying with the wishes of a few crotchetty members of Parliament. The amendment finding no seconder, Dr. MacDormann moved that the minute referring to the accounts be referred back for this reason. He did not know whether the chair-
