RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE SHIP CANAL- . IMPORTANT CLAUSES OBTAINED. The following clauses have been inserted in the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill through the action of the Runcorn Ship Canal Committee : CLAUSES. For the protection of the port and town of Runcorn, and the Improvement Commissioners of the said town (herein- after called the Improvement Commissioners), the follow- ing previsions shall apply, notwithstanding anything in this Act contained to the contrary, that is to say : (1.) In the event of the Company acquiring, under the powers of this Act, the Duke of Briagewater's Canal, from Manchester to Runcorn, or the Runcorn and Weston Canal, or either of them, or the docks and quays at Runcorn be- longing to the Bridgewater Company, and the works in con- nection therewith respectively, they shall not levy or charge any higher tolls, rates or charges for the use thereof respec• tively than are at present levied and charged by the Bridgewater Company; (2) No Canal tolls, or other charge whatsoever, shall be demanded or taken by the Company for any farmyard or stable dung, or for any marl, nightooil, aslipit refuse, cin- ders, or street ewecpings carried by the Improvement Com- missioners, or any of their coatractors, servants, or boatmen on the Canal. or any other Canal acquired by or at the time belonging to the Company, to be used for cultivation of lands within one mile of the Canal, and not otherwise, but in all other cases the Company may demand and take a toll for the carriage thereof not exceediag 01. per ton for any distance. (3.) At the same time as the Company deposit at the office of the Mersey Commissioners, for the approval of such Commissioners, any plans, sections, or working draw- ings, of any work affecting the estuary of the river Mersey, they shall transmit a copy thereof or. the same scale, and also a copy of any accimpanying descriptions or explaua- lions, to the Improvement Commissioners; and it shall be lawful for the Improvement Commissioners, within ten days from the receipt thereof, to make any representations they may think fit to the Mersey Commissioners in respect to such propoeed work, and the manner and extent in and to which it may affect the town and pert of Runcorn ; and the Mersey Commissioners shall consider any such representa- tions if so made. • (4 ) If at any time the entrances or access from the River Mersey to the docks, wharfs, quays, piers. leeks, or landing places at Runcorn, or any of them, shall by reason of the execution of any of the works or operations of the Company be impeded or obstructed, or rendered less deep than before the passing of this Act, the Cempany shall, at their own expense, from time to time, and upon the request of the Improvement Commissienere, or of any aggrieved person or person!, remove or remedy such obstruction or impediment by dredging or otherwise; and the Ickprovent Commission- ers, or any aggrieved persons or person, may rec mer from the Company compensation for damages sustained by them or him during the existence of any obstruction or impedi- ment in such depth of water, and may also remove such obstruction or impediment by dredging or otherwise in Case of default on the part of the Company to do so after they or he shall have given the Company seven days' notice of the existence thereof, and may recover the cost thereof from the Company in any court of competent jurisdiction; and I any dispute respecting any of the matters aforesaid shall be I referred to the arbitrament of the Board of Trade. I (5.)—The company shall not alter, interfere with, Jan age 1 or obstruct any street, road, footpath, sewer, drain or sewer °tidal!, belonging to or Lind* the coati ol of the Improve- ment Commissioners, situate to the west of the entrance to the Canal at Runcorn, and in the event of any such altera- tion, interference, damage or obstruction being at any time caused by the works or operations of the Company, they shall forthwith made good the same, at their own cost, to the reasonable satisfaction of the Improvement Commis- sioners And the Company shall also be liable in compen- sation to such Commissioners for any damage,in jury or loss occasioned to them thereby, such compensation being, in case of dispute, determined y arbitration in the manner provided by the Land Clauses ConsolLation Acts, 1845, 1860, and 1869. (6.) The company•shall at all times afford to the Improve- ment Commissioners all reasonable facilities and accom- modation for carrying through or under the property of the company any sewer, drain or sewer outfall which the Com- missioners may hereafter consider necessary or desirable to construct for the proper drainage of the district, and the company shall allow soch sewers, drains and sewer outialls to be so carried through or under their property without payment of any wayleave or other consideration thereof; provided that any works executed under this subsection shall when and so fir as they affect the Canal or works or other property of the company be carried out according to plans and sections and specifications previously submitted Ito and approved in writing by and under the superinten- dence of the Company's engineer, and shall not interfere with or affect the working of the Canal or the future im- provement thereof, and the Improvement Commissioners snail be liable in compensation to the company for anis- demage, injury or loss occasioned to them by or in con- sequence of any works executed under this subsem ion, such compensation to be determined in case of dispute in the manner provided by the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts 1845,1860 and 1869. (7.) Neither the Company nor their successors shall have any power at any time to nominate or appoint any person or persons to act as a Commissioner or Commissioners under section eleven of the Runcorn Improvement Act, 18.52; and in the event of the Company acquit hag the doci:s, wharves, and landing places in Runcorn belonging to the Bridgewater Company, or any of them, the docks, wharves, and landing places so acquired shalt thenceforth be assessed to the general district rate, or to any other rate for the time keine in force in the district of the Improvement Commissioners in the same manner as other propetty may for the time being be assessable, anything in the provisional order relating to Runcorn, confirmed by the Local Government B lard's Pro- visional Orders Confirmation (Bilbrough, &c.) Act, 1870, contained to the contrary notwithstanding; (8.1 Except as expressly provided by this Act nothing herein contained shall prejudice, alter, or abridge or aff.t.ct any rights, powers, privileges, or authorities of the Im- provement Commissioners unuer any Act of Parliament or otherwise. Agreement relating to deep water channel to be sub- mitted by solicitors for the promoters.

EARLESVOVIN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CRAPEL.—As will be seen from a report in another column, the .Rev. M. Dickenson preached his farewell sermon in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, prior to leaving Rarlestown f()r the Skel- mersdale' circuit. Mr. Dickenson and family d:parted on Tuesday morning. The D•AV resident miniiter will be the Rev, F. N. Shimmiu, formerly of .Manchester.

ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT 'WIDNES. On Saturday, an orange demonstration on a large scale was held at Widnes, the lodges taking part in the proceed- ings being the Widnes Invincibles (110), the Pride of Kirk- dale (251), under the charge of Bro. T. Williams, W.M. ; Ulster Scots 0231, under the charge of Bro. T. Stanley, D.M.; Bootle Invincibles (131), under the charge of Bro. J. Harkness, W.M. This was the first demonstration ever held by the Orange body in Widnes. It is only within the last 18 months that the local lodge has been founded, it always being supposed that the Irish Catholic element was too strong in the town to admit of Orangemen acquiring much influence or numerical strength. The lodge, however, has received an unexpected number of adherents, and it is in contemplation to found a second lodge at Farieworth. This has been taken in hand by Bro. Rev. G. Bond, a locel clergyman of Tory proclivities, who appears to have thrown himself enthusiastically on the side of Orangemen. The fact that no demonstration of thisdescription had previously taken place in the town caused some alarm to the autkori- ties. It was feared that the Catholic and Hibernian population, who naturally are strongly opposed to the opinions held by Orangemen, might attempt some counter demonstration, and that serious disturbances might consequently occur. Every precaution to guard against disturbance and avert catastrophe had therefore been taken. A large extra police force had been drafted into the town from Bootle, Leigh, St. Helens Gers- ten, and Wavertree. Altogether, a force of about 100 con- stables was present. They were under the charge of Colonel Moorson (the chief constable for Lanceshire), Superintendent Barker' and Inspectors Barnett (Widnes), Baxendale (Garston), Keighley (Wavertree), Woods (St. Helens), and Charnley (Leigh). In the earlier hours of the afternoon the streets were filled with people evidently awaiting to see what Kind of a development an Orange demonstration was; though from the fact that very few indeed among the onlookers had donned the familiar Orange lily, it may be concluded that they had no particular sympathy with those who cherished, after their own fashion, the memory of William of Orange. About half- past three the Pride of Kirkdale fife and drum band arrived from Liverpool. The Star of Temperance brass band, whose services had been engaged for the occasion. immedi- ately afterwards put in an appearance. and the two bends proceeded to a piece of waste ground off Dixon-street, where they were joined by the delegates from the Liverpool lodges. Here a procession was formed, headed by Mar- shrills Messrs. Edward Percy and J. W. Woods, who carried drawn swords and were mounted on horseback. The pro- cession was accompanied by the two bands, which played popular "Orange" airs, and by various officers wearing their regalia. Among these may be mentioned Brother William Rankin, Worshipful Master of the Invincible Lodge, Widnes; Brother Mullen, D.M., Brother George Rogerson, Brother T. Carlile, Brother A. Attwell, and Brother Powell. The Bible was carried on a cushion as an emblem of the ad- herence of the Orangemen to the Church of England, and the Charter of the Lodge was carried by the Master and Deputy- Master. We must not omit to mention that a banner, which had recently been purchased by the Widnes Lodge at a cost of .£25, was borne aloft in a conspicuous position. The de- signs upon it were emblematic of Orangeism. On one side was represented King William crossing the Boyne, and the other had been used by the artist to depict the Queen pre- senting a Bible to African princes. At the junction of Vic- toria-road about 60 policemen had been drawn up, presenting a formidable array. As the procession proceeded along they fell in by 2's and 3's amidst its ranks. Thus guarded, the Orangemen marched past the police station up Widnes-road as far as Deacon-road, where the constabulary left them. They then made their way to Farnworth, stopping opposite the Vicarage. The Rev. ciierge Bond c ,nvereed ter some moments With the tame, but try the desire of the Orange. men no address was delivered. Then they returned by the same route to Widnes. No demonstration of any kind occurred, and although between three and four thousand people followed the precession not even a cheer was raised at any point—a fact which would seem to show that Orange principles, though they may have gained a foothold in Widnes, have not yet excited any great degree of enthusiasm. The Widnes vicarage was the next point in the programme of the Orangemen, and to there they proceeded along Victoria and Waterloo-roads. When near Mr. Syred's pawn- broker's shop the first unpleasant incident of the afternoon occurred. A man, named James Crinigan, a dock labourer, who was standing on the footpath, threw a heavy Piece of slag at Edward Percy, one of the marshalls. Mr. Percy saw the act, and drew back his bead, the stone striking his sword and glanced off to the ground. '1 he man was at once taken into custody by P.C. Almond, and on Monday morning was charged at the police court, before Mr. G. Pil- kington and Mr. F. H. Gossage, with committing a breach of the peace. He was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO, and two sureties in £5 each. At Widnes Vicarage, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams conversed a few minutes, but by request no address was delivered. The procession then returned to the Volunteer Hall, where a substantial knife and fork tea was provided, Mr. Collin M`Nab, of Liverpool Steamship and Stewards Catering Company, being the caterer. A meeting attended by nearly one thousand people followed. The Rev. George Bond pre- sided, and he was supported by the Rev. J. Wright-Williams and by the officials of the lodges, whose names we have al- ready given.—The Chairman thanked the orengemen for corning to his house in the afternoon, and p lesed on to con- sider what their principles were and what °ranger:in meant. 1 hey were Orangemen, and as such it was their intention to support the Church and Crewe. And to say that they would support these institutions was not mere words, at a time when they found Ministers in her Majesty's Cabinent talk- ing as they had done lately. It was time, indeed, for them to be earnest in supporting the principles they had at heart. He had joined the Orange body because he liked to see the zeal, and to tee men thoroughly in earnest with what they were about. There were many Conservatives and many members of the Church of England who were pretty well negative Conservatives and negative churchmen. and did not take any active step to promote the principhs they were inteuded to uphold. Earnestness and energy were re- quired. The a adicals and Communists, and other organisa- tions of destructiveness were earnest enough, and worked day and night; but the Conservatives lied churchmen he had mentioned thought that if they let well alone they had done their duty. But this was a mistake. It was not enough to let well alone. If the Radicals showed energy in destroying, the Orangemen must show energy in preserving. (Applause.) But while they showed zeal they should also show discretion. When they exceeded the hounds of dis- cretion they did harm to the cause. They must show moderation and get moderate people to their side—the mederate people who wished to preserve property and desired to maintain the Protestent religion. But they could not hope to do ' this if they tr:ed to carry their own narrow views. There was a great floating mass of people abroad now who might be induced to join the Church and also the Conservative body if they broadened their views, but who would be repelled if any great narrowness was shown. At every general election some- thing of this kind took place, and certainly at the last general election this combined with the bad trade of the time, which made people think any change would be for the better; hence the return of the Liberals to power. Speaking of religious matters, the rev, chairman eaid he way not a Low Churchman nor yet a High Churchman, but he held strongly to the Prayer Bock. People s lid there were no Conservative workingmen, and insisted that a workingman must necessarily be a Radical. There could not be any greater nonsense. Had they read Lord Salisbury's speech the other day at the Conservative Union in London? Toe noble lord had answered the Radical workiagmen who said (het the Liberal party could not be a party to destruction, because there were so many rich men and men who held property in its ranks, and gave ao example of a Prince of France, who joined the Jacobins because he saw no chance of rising lots position in his own party, and afterwards Ip .rished in the common ruin. Many men joined the Opp)- site party merely from pique or some similar cause, and they must remember that some men did not care about wealth who cared for position, and on this ground joined the Radical party. He was struck with the want of cohesion in the present Cabinet. Each man had gone into it for the sake of some foible of his own; they had no c preheneive policy; and when a crisis came first one and then another resigned. A working man might be thought to have no interests to preserve, but this was not the case. Suppose a man established himself in life, got married, and furnished a house, it was to the haerest of that man to be s Conservative. If not how could he tell that B might not say "Yen have acquired seine property, but I have a vote as great as you, and I will vete that we share and share alike." There was no security foe property. There was another point; working men depended on the capital of others, and if someone did not supply material for their work they could have no latroar. If there were no security men would not expend their capital in the employment of labour, but would put it somewhere where it might be secure, say in the funds at three per cent. So that in both tin se points it was to tne interest of working men to be Conserva- tives. As an example of the destrective tendencies of the of the present Government, Mr. Bond referred to what was now taking place in Ireland, where in order to get votes and keep people quiet, Government had reduced the value of landed property one-third, and this meant frightening capital out of the country. Con- servatives were supposed to be the war party but if they would examine history they would find that the Liberals generally made three wars to one made by the Conservatives. He called upon all true Liberals to join the Conservative party, and said the time was coming when every man who desired to maintain the Church and the, Queen would either hive to go on the Con- servative side or else become a Republican. He also con- demned those Liberals who attacked the House of Lords, which ha contended was a great check upon the aggrandise- ment and power of the Crown, a fecteavhich was shown in the reien of Henry VIII., when the Crown gained great power through the nobility having almost died out in the wars of the Roses. The House of Lords was a kind of con- , uecting link between the Crown and tho people, and had prevented premature legislation o hich would have proved very disruptive to the goo lof the country. In conclusion, he charged the present Government with haying got into power by flattering the prejudices and pandering to the Irma passions of the multitude.—The Rev. J. Wright Williams, who was received with loud and centinued applause,thanked those preKnt for the hearty rec,ption they. had given him, end congratulatentiern upon the successful work they bad done since their last meeting, and more especially titian 0h0:41h,, the presence of the H- v. George Bond in the chair, and upon the decoration which he wore. (howl ap- plause..) If he (Mr. Williams) had not et present their badge upon his bre,:t ho should give way t..)

in the respect he had for the principles that that badge represented. He recalled the time of William of Orange, and reminded the audience that that King had delivered them from the domination of the bitter biting heel, which he who once felt never forgot, and though that face might be now behind the mask the face was there. The motto of Rome they must rfbt forget was still seniper eadein. —Bro. Wm. Rank, W.1V1., also gave a short address, in which he alluded to the progress Orangeism had made in the locality.—A number of recitations and songs were given by the members of the Order, and the proceedings terminated about half-past ten.

GOSSIP OF THE LONDON CORRESPON- DENT. It was stated on Thursday in the lobby that Mr. Brad- laugh's speech on Wednesday night, so far as it referred to Mr. Chaplin, would be brought under the notice of the Speaker. That, however, has not been done, and it is said that Sir Henry Brand is of opinion that the matter is not one in which the House should concern itself. It is coming home to the Church party that nothing has really been gained by the defeat of the Deceased Wife's Sis;ter Bill. They have rejected their own compromise, and it will never be offered to them again. Next year, when the bill re-appears, it will insist upon the right of sisters-in-law to be married in their parish churches if they can obtain a clergyman to perform the ceremony; and will forbid any clergyman to deny the communion to such as contract these unions. The Irish members have discovered a new way of wreak- ing vengeance on their enemies. They do. not usually vote on private Bills, but on Thursday afternoon Mr. Ainsworth, who voted consistently for the Coercion Bill, moved the re- jection of the Ennerdale Railway Bill. Mr. Forster supported the motion for the rej-ction, and immediately the rarnellites collected their forces and voted for the Bill. The result was that Mr. Ainsworth and Mr. Forster were de- feated by seven votes. Mr. Childers saves £4,700 by his support of Mr. Stansfeld's r..solution against the C.D. Acts. Last year the administra- tion of the law cost £13,565. This yea: the Exchequer will have to bear the burden of £8,865. An amended estimate has been issued, which shows that the money now asked for is to he spent only on hospitals. So that though the health of the population may suffer, the Exchequer will benefit— which perhaps justifies our retrograde action in the eyes of an economical Chancellor of the Exchequer. Not much objection is likely to be taken by the opponents of the Government to the payment of a heavy annual subsidy to the Aineer of Afghanistan, though it iv rather odd that such an arrangement should be made under the Gladstoae rims. The Liberal policy with regard to Afghanistan has of late been to let it alone, and to have as little as poseible to do with it. But the grant of a large subsidy would seem to show that this doctrine is held in a very louse way. Pertiaps the Liberals have come to see at last the truth of the observation that either Russia or England must be supreme at Cabul, and they have resolved that it will not be he former.

A curious incident that happened the other evening is worthy of being noted. There was a large party at the house of a leading lady in fashionable life, and the conversition ran, as it has done very much lately, on the subject of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill. Many of the ladies were speak- ing against and some in favour of the measure, when the hostess, half by way of a joke, proposed that a division should take place on the subject. 'lbis was done, when it was found that of 67 ladies present 23 were against and 44 in favour of the bill becoming law, thus showing that all the fair sex are not, as has been said, antagonistic to the proposed change. Tlae results of the division surprised those present as well as those who heard of it afterwards not a little. The Channel Tunnel Committee meet on Tuesday to con- sider their report. The result will leave the matter pretty much where it is at present. As I stated here some time since, the draft report of Lord Lansdowne will be favour- able, and that of Sir Hussey Vivian adverse. Mr. Baxter and probably Lord Aberdare will be favourable; others will side against the project. it is thought that it will appear when the Joint Committee has reported that the prospects of the p•oject are absolutely unaffected by the labours of that dis- tinguished body. There will be an increase of Tunnel literature, and that will be nearly all. The consideration of the nature of the official understanding with the French Government will be set forth more clearly than in any previous publication; but after all the question will have to be tried by public opinion, and there is nothing whatever to bind the will of Parliament. The " secretary" of Mrs. Woodhull, "candidate for the Presidency of the United States for 1884," has circulated a printed " " " from free England supported by English capitalists." This most ridiculous document goes on to state that Mrs. Woodhull is " ready with all her wonted devotion to her country and to the cause of humanity to take this work upon herself, and gives unreservedly all her strength, enthusiasm, and all the wealth she has accumu- lated in England to the result of this election." It con- tinues: " All chosen delegates will be provided with free return tickets by steamer from Philadelphia or New York and Boston, and during the attendance at the three days' Convention will have all expenses paid for them. The meetings for the nomination will be held at St. James's Hall." .

I should not be surprised if the statements made in both Houses of Parliament the other day on the annexation pro- jects of the Australian colonies should be the first step in a vries which may lead to the loss of these vigorous commu- nities to the Crown. We are already informed that the speech of Lord Derby has caused great dissatisfaction, the colonists feeling as if they had been snubbed in a matter about which they were better judges than the Colonial Minister. I doubt very much whether Queensland will abandon the policy she has so boldly adopted or consent to see the Dutch or the French found naval establishments on the other side of the Torres Straits. It wih be seen, too, that the treatment of the colonies by the mother country iutl th.m in mr.nornt movement for annexation, and psrheps their own confederation. It needs only under the present rath :r exciting circumstances a bold speech froni a popular politician to precipi ate an agitation for iudependence. Mr. Alfred Austin explains. He was said to have claimed nine-tenths of the literary power of England for the Tories. according to the reports, he claimed Mr. Froude, who never could stand Lord Beaconsfield's Imperialism ; Mr. Matthew Arnald, who has alvvays been a possible Liberal candidate, and many other men hardly lees Liberal. Bat it seems that he did nOthirot of the sort. He only slid that these men were called Liberal, but they, had some Conservative ten- dencies. If this method of judgment is to be permitted, there will be no, Liberals left save Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Jesse Collings. Mr. Gladstone has some Conservative tendencies. The Lord Chancellor has a great many. Mr. Bright is not free from a certain suspicion.. Mr. Ferster will be taken as a Tory out and out, and Mr. Goschen will be worse. Turn this method about, and the only true Tory will be Mr. Warton. Led Salisbury is Liberal on the cpiestion of the school curriculum, en dwel- lings for the working classes, and on questions of a purely social charactei; Sir Stafford Northcote on many matters. Lord Randolph Churchill is a Railed. Mr. Gorst has only one conviction. The single thread of p-inciple with which h., covers his nakedness is that we ought to be just to native races—a Radical doctrine. Mr. Alfred Austin had better not have explained. He seemed only presumptuous at first, and it is the right of a pact to be presumptuous. Now he talks simply nonsense. Perhaps it is the right of a poet to be nonsensical. One result of the death of the Doke of Marlborough will be to make Lady Blandford Duchess of Marlborough for a few weeks. She at present possesses the title, but the decree of divorce will become absolute presently, and she will then become again Lady Alberta Hamilton. Her son, the future duke, was under the guardianship of the late duke. He will now become the ward of the Duke of Abercorn. It is a curious fact that the Duke of Marlborough has lived only just long enough to conclude the sale of the art troesures of Blenheim Palace. In explanation of this step it has ben said that he made haste to sell them eft because he knew that his son an 4 heir would do so as soon as he came to power. The death of the duke places another Garter at the disposal of the Premier—that is to say, it is constitutionally in the gift of the Prime Minister, but it is understood that just now the Sovereign insists upon person- ally and actually disposing of this blue ribbon of political life. The Duke of Marlborough will perhaps be the best remem- bered by the letter addressed to him by the Earl of Beacons- field on the eve of the general election in 1880, in which. the Prime Minister raised a warning voice regarding the machin- ations of the Irish separatists, and spoke of peace as resting "on the presence, not to say the ascendency, of England in the councils of Europe." It is rather singular that the Marquis ef Blandford, who succeeds to the dukedoine is a Liberal, if not a Radicalrend came forward a year or two ago to contest Cambridgeshire against the Tories, but withdrew before the elsction for reasons partly financial and warily in consequence of a scandal with which his name had. been un- fortunately mixed up. It is well known that the political opinion of his heir gave much concern to the Duke, isle° on the other hand always expressed his gratification at the sand made by his younger son, Lord Randolph Churchill, on the Conservative side of the House of Cornmorm

div.head: ANNUAL INSPECTION OF- WIDNES LOC IL BOARD.
div.p: ANNUAL INSPECTION OF- WIDNES LOC IL BOARD.

AN ACCIDENT OCCURS. The commendable custom et once a year inspecting those valuible and extensive undertakings, the Gas and Water Works, which are carried on for the public good, was ob- served by the members of Widnes Local Board on Thursday. The common meeting place was the offices in Aiforde Chambers, and those members who had arrived at the rendezvous at a quarter-pass eleven proceeded to the Gas Works on foot in a shower of rain, which seemed to augur still dirtier weather before the day's proceedings had con- cluded. At the gas office the party was met by Mr. Carr, the manager, who at once assumed the duties of guide, and fulfilled them with complete satisfaction to all concerned. The yard, the etorerootns, the smithy, and the retort houses were all visited, and Mr. Carr had the pleasure of pointing out and describing to the members a number of alterations and improvements he had been instrumental in introducing during his, as yet, short reign over the establishment. His administrative capacity and practical ability are testified to by the large profit on the works, to which we referred a short time ago, and still better results are anticipated for the future. A new apparatus introduced is the tank for the purpose of testing water meters. This will enable the Board to deal fairly with all consumers by, on complaiut,discover- ing defects in the :aim, if there are any, and thus setting all doubts at rest. But the greatest innovation is taking place in the retort houses. Owing to the intense heat to which these cylindrical vessels are subjected, they become burnt out and require replacing every few months. As these renewals occur, Mr. Carr is having the retorts con- structed on a new principle. which will effect great economy. especially in the censumption of fuel. To those desirious of knowing, Mr. Carr explained that were it requisite the works could produce a million and a half cubic feet of gas per day, but the highest maximum daily make at the pre- see time, he pointed out, had not exceeded 400,000 cubic, feet while the yearly average was not more than 72 million cubic feet. Mr. Pankhurst, the chairman of the Gas and Water Committee, also aided the party in their in- spection by directing their attention to various points of interest in the recondite action of the apparatus they were viewing. Returning to Alforde Chambers, an open drag, to which was harnessed three horses, and a cab, drawn by a couple of similar animals of a more diminutive build, were found to be in readiness to convey the party farther afield. These were from the stables of Mr. Fowler, of the Central Hotel, Widnes. Again, as at the last inspection, the mem- bers had to regret the absence of Mr. F. H. Gossage, the re- spected chairman of the Board, the only other absentee being Mr. W. H. Kershaw. The members who therefore took their seats in the conveyances were—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, J. Midwood, D. Forster, F. H. Pankhurst, S. Sadler, D. Wright, J. E. Johnson, E. Martley, Richard Webster, J. Houghton, and B. Dutton. The officials—Mr. J. T. Allen (clerk), Mr. Carr (gas and water manager), Mr. Higginson (sur- veyor), Mr. Dickson (nuisance inspector), and three reporters made up the rest of the party. Their heads turned in the direction of Widnes-road, the horses quickly pro- ceeded through Farnivorth to Pes Hill. The rain had ceased, and the sun's beams breaking through the dark cloads lighted up the areen and verdant landscape with increasine brightness as Widnes, hidden in the grimy emanations of its numerous tall chimneys, was left further behind. At Pex Hill, which has a considerable elevation above sea level, the covered reservoirs of the waterworks are situated, from whence the view obtained is magnificent; and the ob- jects of the excursion attained,the party inhaled, with percep- tible enjoyment, the pure health-giving oxogen of bracing bre: ze, and admired the scene unfolded to their view—a valley of emerald meadows and dark-cested coppices, edged with that broad and silvery stream, the Mersey, behind which reared the lofty mountains of Wales. In an outbuilding on the hill lunch was partaken of, and then the journey was continued to Stockswell, which has been previously described in The Evanziner. After a short stay here the nicturesque pump- ing station at Netherley was visited. The magnificent and powerful engine was at work, and its action was much ad- mired. The ponderous machinery at the well's mouth was examined, and surprise was expressed at the vast volume of water which was raised at each stroke, being no less than 130 gallons. -Mr. Carr, who had continued his good offices as guide, here produced plans for the erection of a brick building over the old pumping engine "Swan," the esti- mated cost of the erection being £6OO. At present the machinery has only a wooden covering. A visit to a well at Belle Vale brought the business of the day to a close, and orders were given to drive on to Childwall Abbey, which was reached shortly before four o'clock. At the quaint Abbey Hotel the party sat down to a knife and fork tea, en i the inner min saltenea, the vielaere °per, the evening ie :lie beautiful grounds which are attached to the hotel, and ate.nce a be tutiful prospect is afforded to the gaze A quarter to nine arrived, and the party, whose num- b -r had been reduced to twelve,several gentleman leaving re- turned home by train, took their seats in the drag. The conveyance had not been moved more than a few yards, when it stopped, and a cry was raised that a horse was down. There was a hurried exit from the carriage, and a somewhat excited grouping round the horses. One of the animals, like time minstrel who published his poetieal effusions, was, it was stated, " lazy," and had Wilfully laid down in the road, causing 11.9 companion in harness ti shy, and breaking the carriage pole. Fortunately the animal quickly got upon its legs, or it is not improbabie the cenveyance would have been overturned, and a pleasant day had a sad ending. After consultation, the driver was de- spatched to Wootton for a pole. the horses returned to the stable, and the visitors to the hotel to pass the time as best they mierht. About an hour elapsed before the return of the driver with the pole, which it was then discovered would not fit, but after half an hour's hammering and chipping it was knocked into posHon, but the bolt by which it should be fixed could not be inserted. However, it was declared safe, and at half-past ten the party re-entered the carriage. Fortunately, aPhough the moon hid her face, her pile beams illuminated the road, lessening the difficulties of driving; and a start was made. Not anticipating so late a drive, most of the occupants had not provided themselves with overalls, and the slight shudderings of apprehension as to the safety of the pole changed into shiverings of cold as the journey progressed apace ; and a cold wind blew upon them. Happily no further accident occurred, and Widnes was reached a few minutes before midnight, the party exchang- ing congratulations as they senarated. TREAT TO TR INMAT FS OF DUrION WORKEIOUSE AT -HALTON- By the kind invitation of the Rev. Edward and Mts. Marsden, the whole of time iror,ates. of the Runcorn Union Workhouse were, on Wednesday, treated to an excellen t tea and given a days enjoyment, which must have proved a welcome change in the monotony of their lives. The inmates, to the number of 170 were conveyed in waggens, lent by the neighbouring farmers, from the Workhouse to Halton, where they were met by Mr. and M!-s. Marsden and the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar of Halton. At the girls' schoolroom a splendid knife - and -fork tea eras held, the substantial fare being richly enjoyed. The juvenile portion of the party joined in a variety of games in a field lent by Mr. Stokes, of the Prospect Farm; while the old people strolled through the viLlae, surveying the fine prospect from the ruins which crown the hill. At half-pest six the party again assembled in the schoolroom, when a short address was delivered by the Rev. E. Marsden, chaplain of the workhouse. He rem irked that that was elle day out of the 365 in the year upon which they enjoyed themselves; and, as one old person not long age remarked to him, "they hed had a very happy time, and thank Clod for it." Oa behalf of Mrs. Ma.raden and himsolf, he thanked the Vicar of Halton for his kindness in allowing them the use of his school, and for having taken such a personal interest in the work of the day, which had tended to tasks them so happy and comfortable.—The Rev. John Lockwood also addressed the party, and ex- pressed the pleasure it was to him to receive the people in his parish, and especially in his schools. They must all, indeed, feel very grateful to Mr. and Mrs. Marsden for their kindness oa all occasions, and for their hospitality on that. After offering some words of counsel and advice, the Vicar called for three cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Marsden.—The re- quest was ve-y heartily responded to ; and cheers having been given for Mr. and Mrs. Jones, master and matron of the Ilouse, the company sang the Dox alogy ; and afterwards dep tined for the Workhouse in the conveyances which had brought them to Halton.

div.head: WOUNDED BY A SAUCEPAN AT WIDNES. \
div.p: WOUNDED BY A SAUCEPAN AT WIDNES. \

At Widnes Police Court, en Tuesday, before Mr-. John Block, Harriet Burns, a married woman, was brought up in custody charged with unlawfully and maliciously wound- ing Mary Lightfoot.—lt appeared from the evldende of Elizabeth Partington, of 2, Holfmd-street, that on the pre- vious afternoon a dispute arose between the prosecutris and 1 the prisoner with regard to the Orange procession, one of the disputants being.a Catholic and the other belng an adherent of the Orange body. From words they came to blows, and Mrs. Burns seized a saucepan and struck Mrs. Lightfoot a viotent blow on the head. With such force did she strike her that the saucepan was broken in three pieces, 1 and injuries of a very serious nature were inflicted upon the prosecutris who was rendered insensible, and lost a great deal of bloOl. She was removed home, and Mrs. Partington's husband gave information to the police.—Dr. Cooper stated that he was called in to see the injured woman, and found she was sufferiog from two wounds on the bead. She was quite unable to appear at court that day, and he could not say what the result of the assault would be. Mrs. Light- foot had lost some blood.—The prisenerwas remanded until Friday.—The prieorier was again brought before the magi- :rates yesterday, bat the prosecutrix was too weak to appear and give evidenc.e, The prizoner was ceeee.quently egairs remanded. -

div.head: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS.

These sessions were opened at the Castle, Chester, on Monday, before the Chairman, Lord Egerton of 'fatten, and the Deputy-Chairman, Mr. Horkttio Lloyd.—The Deputy- Chairman, addressing the grand jury, congratulated them on the satisfactory state of the calendar, there being only seven prisoners for trial, as against eighteen for trial at the same time last year. Of these eighteen however, six had belonged to the borough of Birkenhead': which had since been made into a separate criminal jurisdiction, so that the. proper figures to compare were seven and twelve, still show-. ing a gratifying condition of affairs. The court met in tict grand jury room for the transaction of county business, the chait man presiding. The Chief Constable, Lieutenant- Colonel Hamersley, submitted a return of crime for the quarter ended 31sLMay, which gave a total of 264 appre- hended and summoned, of whom. 55 were committed, for trial, 2 257 summarily convicted, and 809 discharged In comparison- with the 'corresponding quarter of last year there was a decrease of 27 apprehended, and an increase of 295 summoned, 468, persons having been proceeded against - under the Education Act-. The payments for the quarter commencing were estimated at :4.6407 ss, anti to meet this a county rate of 2d in the pcned, produc- ing £19,791 18s was ordered. A police rate of one-eighth of a penny, producing 41,085 13e 10d was also, ordered , Mr. James Tomkinson proposed, in pursuancauf notice, that it was expedient to rearrange the number of, polling districts :and polling places for the Pargumentary division of West Cheshire, and that the following should be the polling places :—Alsager, Audlart., Birkenhead, Bun- bury, Chester, Christleton, Crewe, Dunham-n'- the-Hill, Eccieston, Eddisbury' Farndon, Frodsham, lies- wall,' es- wall, loose, Kingsley Liscard,Malpas, ".antwich, Neston, New Ferry, Ouston, Over, Poulton-cnmeacombe, -Great 8 tughall, Great Sutton, Tarporley, Tarvin, Tranmere, 1 ;'atteohall, Unten, Uotou-byeelwater, Weaverham, and Wrenhury. man of the committee had taken the trouble to make him- self familiar with the fact that the Board was paying an inspector £lO a year, and that the money came out of the pockets of the Runcorn rate- payers, who were ;not boat-owners. The chair- man of the committee had made a most misleading speech. He said distinctly that he did not wish the burdens of these boat-people to be increased. He (Dr. MacDougall) said the same thing, but why should individuals who were not boat-owners have to bear the burden? The Bill pro- vided for an annual payment by the boat-owners for the payment of any charges arising from the administration of the Act.—Mr. FISHER said he was aware that an inspector was paid, but the doctor would find that not one penny had Yet come out of the ratepayers' pockets.—The SECRETARY said since the passing of the Act the amount realised from registration fees was £lOO. Of that there had been spent about £l2O, leaving about £7O, which had been put to the credit of the Board. There had been £5O paid for inspec- tion of boats, so that left a balance, if they had kept it dis- tinct from the rate, of about £25. The annual amount re- ceived now for registration of boats was about '£2 10e., or £7 10s. short of the inspector's salary.—Dr. MecDoyeetet was glad that explanation had been made, and expressed himself satisfied that the course which the committee had thought proper to take was inimical to the best interests of the ratepayers.—Mr. LASE, in order that the discussion might be exhausted, seconded the amendment. It seemed to him that the Beard, having received the fees from the canal boats, must expect to pay the piper, but he saw no objection to getting the money out of the Imperial Exchequer. He thought, however, that they would not be successful in that, but there was no harm in asking for it.—Mr. SHAW had noticed that there had been a great outcry throughout the country against the interference of the Local Government Board officials, and that really lay at the root of this ques- tion. If the clause was struck out and the parties in Lon- don bad to pay the costs he did not think they would have so many investigations, and he did not think the Board should do anything to cause further interference in the con- duct of public affairs by the Local Government Board.— The amendment was lost and the minutes declared carried. FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for June amounted to £9lB Bs. 2d., and recommended accounts amounting to £499 ss. Bd. It was also recommended that the mortgage of £125, due to the trustees of the Parish Church Organ Fund on July let, 1883, be paid off.—Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. SPF.AKMAN seconded, the adoption of the minutes, which were, after some discussion, passed. WATERLOO HOUSE. The CHAIRMAN moved the following resolution of which had given notice :—" That the resolution passed at a meeting of the Commissioners, held on January 17th, 1883, adopting the report of the Waterloo House Committee, as to the appropriation and allotment of the rooms in Waterloo House be rescinded, and that the matter be referred to the said committee for further consideration, and for such amended recommendations as they may think it advisable to make."—The CHAIRMAN explained that this resolution was necessary in order that the committee might meet the wishes of the Library Committee and other public bodies in regard to one or two rooms.—Mr. PRITCHAUD seconded the motion.—Dr. MacDomeaee said he understood from the public prints that the committee were allowing a certain public body the use of rooms at Waterloo House free of charge for 41 years. He did not know whether that was true or not.—Mr. Seeeev replied that the committee had not committed the Board to anything of the kind. They could only make a recommendation, and the Board could adopt it or otherwise.—The motion was passed.—Letters from the School Board and the Overseers, with regard to Waterloo House, were referred to the committee.—The meeting then terminated.

- FOR-,T SHILLINGS AND COSTS FOR STEALING SIXPENNY won= WlRE—Before H. Blecklv, R. Houghton, and A. C. McCorquodale, E3qrs., at Newton Town Hall, on Saturday sat, Edward Hodson. farmer, of Buttonwood, was charged with stealing, on the Mtla of May, 13 yards of wire fencing, value 6d, the property of Robert Kilshall. of Brad- ley Hall, Burtonwood. The defendant was defended by Mr. Marsh, of St. Helens.—P.S. Commins stated that he was en duty on a footpath leading from Earlestown to the centre of Buttonwood, und when passing a place known as Bradley Wood, he saw the defendant pulling the wire produced out of a hedge. He (witness) waited until the man had finished when he saw him proceed to coil it round the stump of a tree and attempted to put it in his pocket. He (wit- ness) then went up to him and said" What are yot . thing with that ? " The man appeared to be somewhat surprised, And turning roundquickley, he replied. "I wanted a bit of wire and I thought I would take it, Mr. Commins." He was asked if he had any permission to take it, and he replied that he had not.—Mr. Kilshaw, the occupier of the land in question, said he had been in communication with Mr. Brooks, of Manchester, the owner, who had given instruc- tions for the defendant to be proceeded againet.—The de- fendant was fined 40s and costs. FRODSHA.M.

PARISH CHURCH CHOIR TRIP.—The annual trip of the Frodshim Parish Church Choir tolk place on Thursday, to Southport. Toe weather in the early part of the day was somewhat threatening, but it cleared up in the at ternoon and a very pleasant day was spent. MARRIAGE OF THE RE7. D. SCHOFIELD AT FRODSHAM —On Thursday the marriage of the Rev. Daniel Schofield, Primitive Methodist Minister, to Miss Euphemia Catherine Borwick, daughter of the Rev. R. P. Borwick, of the Manor House Academy, Frodsharuf took place at the Trinity Wes- leyan Chapel, Frodsham. The chapel was well filled for _

aome time before the wedding partj arrived, and much in- terest was taken in the happy event as the bride and bride- groom have won many friends since they came to Frodsham. Miss Borwick was accompanied by her uncle Mr. W. Mel- rose, who performed the ceremony of giving the bride away. She wore a handsome dress of brown satin, trimmed with brochO, with bridal veil and orange blossoms. The brides- maids were Miss Euphemia Bur wick (cousin of the bride), and Miss Lammie, of Weldon, Northampton, who were at- tired in grey poplin dresszs trimmed with satin. The father _

of tht';- 'bride, the R. P. Borwick, was the offl?' I`;ng minister, he being assisted by the Williams, of Runcorn, and the Rev. A. Kirkland, of Al. rincharn. On leaving the chapel. the organist played the Wedding March, and the bride and bridegroom received the congratulations of their friends, After the re- gister had been signed, the newly-married couple walked down the aisle of the chapel, which had been strewn with floral tributes by their numerous well-wishers, and the pro- verbial rice was freely bestowed. The presents were nu me rous and costly. _

TITE PARISH ACCOUNTS.—A statement of the accounts of the Parochial Schools, Clothing Society, Choir Fund, Diocesan Board of Education, National Society, Missionary Association, and Lymm Female Benefit Society, for the past year has just been issued, and a summary may not be found devoid of interest. It shows that the total receipts in con- nection with the Parochial Schools for the year ending May 31st last amounted to £923 3s 21 (less £361 4s 6d, balance in hand on June Ist last year), and the payments to £592 2s Old, leaving a balance of £331 is lid in the bank. The subscriptions to these arnountEd to £62 10s. For the Clothing Society the total receipts were £lBB 3s 2d (less £1 is 2d, balance in hand in November, 1882), and the pay- ments to £lBB 8s sd, so that there is a balance of 5s 3d due to the treasurer. The total receipts of the Choir Fund amounted to £24 10s 2d (less £3 12s 6td, balance in hand in January, 1882), and the payments to £2O lls Gd, leaving a balance of £3 18s 9d in hand. The offertories to the Chester Diocesan Board of Education, which gives aid to the schools in poor parishes,- and provides inspectors in religious knowledge for all Church of England schools in the diocese of Chester, amounted to £7 5a 21; while those to the National Society, whose object is the promotion of the education of the poor in the principles of the Estab- lished Church, amonnted to £6 15s Gd. The Missionary Association receipts were £2l 2s 6d. The Lymm Female Benefit Society's account showed the receipts to be £24108 lid (less £5 13s 2d, balance in hand in January, 1882), while the payments were £3O 6s; and £l7 having been withdrawn from the Savings' Bank, there is a balance of £ll 4s lid in hand; the account at the Warrington Savings' Batik show- ing an amount of £525 03 ad to the credit of the society.

"DRUNK AND DRY."—A man named Patrick Gately was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday last, with begging in Church-street, on Saturday.—Prisoner de- nied that be was begging, but said he was so drunk and dry that he went into a public-house to get a glass of beer. I—He1—He was sent to gaol for seven days.
